name: 2 Kings
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Once Ahab was dead, the land of Moab{a} broke away from Israel’s rule.

In Samaria, King Ahaziah fell through the wooden screen of his upstairs room and was badly hurt. So he sent men off with this message: “Go to Ekron{c} and ask Baal-zebub,{b} its god, if I am going to get better.”

Then the angel of Yahweh spoke to Elijah from Tishbe. “Get going,” he said. “Go out on the road and stop the messengers sent by Samaria’s king. Ask them, ‘Has Israel run out of God? Is that why you are on your way to ask Baal-zebub, Ekron’s god?’
So here is Yahweh’s message for the king: ‘You climbed into that bed, and you will never climb out of it. Death is coming for you.’” Then Elijah left.
The king’s men came back early. “What are you doing here?” he asked.

They said, “A man met us on the road. He told us to turn around and give you a message: ‘Yahweh says, “Is there no God in Israel, that you send men to ask Baal-zebub, Ekron’s god? Since you did that, the bed under you now is the bed you will die in. You will not rise from it.”’”
The king asked, “This man who stopped you and said all this, what did he look like?”
They answered, “He wore a coat of hair{d} and had a leather belt around his middle.” “Elijah from Tishbe!” said the king. “It was him.”

The king sent an officer with his company of fifty soldiers to bring Elijah back. They found the prophet seated on a hilltop. The officer called up to him, “Man of God! The king orders you down here.”

Elijah answered the officer, “If I really am a man of God, then may fire drop out of heaven and eat you up, along with all fifty of your soldiers!” Down came the fire. It burned up the officer and his company.
So the king sent a second officer, again with fifty soldiers. This one shouted, “Man of God, these are the king’s orders: come down right now!”
Elijah said, “If I am truly God’s man, let fire come from the sky and destroy you and your fifty.” Again God’s fire fell. It burned up that officer and his whole company too.

Then the king sent a third officer with fifty men. This officer climbed the hill and dropped to his knees before Elijah. He begged, “Man of God, please think of my life, and the lives of these fifty men who serve you, as worth something.
Twice fire has come from the sky and wiped out the officers who came before me and all their men. But please, spare my life.”
The angel of Yahweh said to Elijah, “Go with him. You do not need to be afraid of him.” So Elijah stood up and went with the officer to the king.

Elijah told the king, “Here is what Yahweh says: ‘You sent men off to Ekron to ask its god Baal-zebub, as though Israel had no God who could answer you. Because of that, you will never leave the bed you are in. You will die.’”
And Ahaziah died, just as Yahweh had said through Elijah. He had no son, so Jehoram{e} became king next. At that time Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat was in his second year as Judah’s king.{f}
Everything else Ahaziah did is recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings.{g}

notes.text: Moab was the land east of the Dead Sea. People explained the name as “from father” (Genesis 19:37).
Baal-zebub means “lord of flies.” It was probably a mocking change of Baal-zebul, “Baal the prince.” The Septuagint calls him “Baal Fly.”
Ekron was one of the five Philistine cities. Its name means “uprooting” or “barren place.”
Or “he was a hairy man.” The Hebrew says “a lord of hair.”
Jehoram (also spelled Joram) means “Yahweh is lifted up.”
The Septuagint does not have the words in this verse after “as Yahweh had said through Elijah.” Compare 3:1, which says Jehoram of Israel began to rule in Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth year.

The Hebrew says “the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.” The Septuagint adds a short summary of Jehoram’s rule here: he ruled twelve years, did evil but not as much as his mother, removed Baal’s stone pillars, but kept the sins of Jeroboam.

subheads.1: King Ahaziah Asks the Wrong God

verses.text: The time came when Yahweh was going to lift Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elijah and Elisha were leaving Gilgal.{a}

Elijah said, “Stay here, Elisha. Yahweh is sending me to Bethel.”{b} But Elisha said, “As surely as Yahweh lives, and as surely as you live, I will not leave your side.” So both of them went down to Bethel.
Bethel was home to a group of prophets. They came out and asked Elisha, “Did you know that Yahweh will take your master away from you today?”{c} “I know,” he said. “Do not talk about it.”
Then Elijah said, “Elisha, wait here. Yahweh is sending me to Jericho.” Elisha answered, “I promise by Yahweh’s life and yours, I will not leave you.” So they went on to Jericho.
The group of prophets in Jericho came up to Elisha. “Your master will be taken from you today. Yahweh is going to do it,” they said. “Did you know?” He said, “Yes, I know. Be quiet about it.”
Elijah said again, “Please stay here. Now Yahweh wants me at the Jordan.” Elisha replied, “By the life of Yahweh, and by your life too, I will stay with you.” So the two kept walking together.
Fifty men from the group of prophets went along. They stood and watched from far off while Elijah and Elisha stopped at the Jordan.
Elijah rolled up his coat and hit the river with it. The water split apart, part to the right and part to the left. The ground under the river was dry, and they crossed on it.
On the other side, Elijah spoke. “Soon I will be taken from you. What would you like me to do for you first?” Elisha answered, “I ask for a double share{d} of your spirit.”
“That is a hard thing to ask,” Elijah said. “But if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. If you do not see me, it will not.”
They kept walking along and talking. All of a sudden a fiery chariot and fiery horses rushed between the two men. And a whirlwind carried Elijah up to heaven.

Elisha watched it happen. He kept shouting, “My father! My father! You were Israel’s chariots and horsemen!” Then Elijah was gone from sight. Elisha grabbed his own clothes and ripped them in two pieces.
Elijah’s coat had fallen off him. Elisha picked it up, went back to the Jordan, and stood at the edge of the water.
He hit the water with the coat that had fallen from Elijah. “Where is Yahweh, Elijah’s God?” he cried. As he struck the water, it split to the right and the left, and Elisha walked across.{e}
The prophets from Jericho were watching from the other side.{f} “The spirit that was on Elijah now rests on Elisha!” they said. They hurried out to him and bowed with their faces to the ground.

“Sir,” they said, “we have fifty strong men here who serve you. Please send them out to search. The Spirit of Yahweh may have carried your master off and dropped him on a mountaintop or down in a valley.” Elisha told them, “Do not send them.”
But they kept begging until he felt too embarrassed to keep saying no. “All right, send them,” he said. So fifty men searched for three days. They could not find Elijah.
Elisha was still in Jericho when they came back. He said, “I told you not to go, didn’t I?”
Some men from Jericho came to Elisha. “Sir,” they said, “this city sits in a fine place, as you can tell. Yet the water is bad, and the land makes babies die before birth.”{g}
“Bring me a new bowl,” Elisha said. “Fill it with salt.” They did.

Elisha went out to the spring where the water came from and tossed in the salt. He said, “Yahweh says, ‘I have made this water healthy. It will not bring death anymore, and babies will not be lost because of it.’”
The water has stayed good ever since, as Elisha had said.
From Jericho, Elisha went up the road toward Bethel. A crowd of young boys{h} ran out of the town and started mocking him. “Go away, baldy!” they shouted. “Go on up, bald head!”
Elisha turned and looked at them. Then he called down a curse on them in Yahweh’s name. Two mother bears charged out of the forest. They mauled forty-two of those boys.
Elisha went on to Mount Carmel. Later he went back to Samaria.

notes.text: Gilgal means “circle (of stones).” This Gilgal was probably in the hills north of Bethel, not the one near Jericho.
Bethel means “house of God.”
The Hebrew says “from over your head,” meaning from being your master. The same is true in verse 5.
The Hebrew says “a mouth of two.” This was the share an oldest son received from his father (Deuteronomy 21:17).
Some readers join the Hebrew words for “he too” with the question: “Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah, indeed?”
The Hebrew says “from opposite.”
Or “the land is barren.” The same Hebrew word is in verse 21.
The Hebrew words can mean young boys or young men.

verses.text: Ahab’s son Jehoram took the throne of Israel in Samaria when Jehoshaphat had been ruling Judah for eighteen years. Jehoram stayed king for twelve years.
Yahweh saw the evil that Jehoram did. Yet his parents had done worse than he did. He removed the stone pillar for Baal that his father had set up.
But Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into sin, and Jehoram held tight to those same sins. He never gave them up.
Mesha,{a} Moab’s king, kept large flocks of sheep. He owed Israel’s king a yearly payment of 100,000 lambs, plus the wool from 100,000 rams.
After Ahab died, though, Moab’s king refused to obey Israel’s king any longer.
So King Jehoram left Samaria and gathered the whole army of Israel for war.

He sent word to Jehoshaphat, who ruled Judah: “Moab’s king is in revolt and will not obey me. Would you march out with me to fight Moab?” Jehoshaphat sent back, “Yes, I will come. Count me as one with you. My soldiers and my horses are yours to use.”
Jehoshaphat asked, “Which way should we attack?” Jehoram said, “We will take the road through the desert of Edom.”{b}

So Israel’s king set out, with Judah’s king and Edom’s king beside him. They took a long, roundabout way. After seven days of marching, there was no water left for the soldiers or for the animals that came with them.
Israel’s king cried out, “This is terrible! Yahweh has brought us three kings out here just to let Moab capture us!”

But Jehoshaphat said, “Surely one of Yahweh’s prophets is around here. Then we could ask Yahweh through him.” One of Israel’s officers spoke up. “Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He was Elijah’s helper. He used to pour water on Elijah’s hands for washing.”
“He speaks Yahweh’s word,” Jehoshaphat said. So the three kings, of Israel, Judah and Edom, went down to the prophet.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, “Why should I help you?{c} Go ask the prophets your father and mother listened to!” Israel’s king answered, “No! It is Yahweh who brought the three of us here, to give us to Moab.”
Elisha said, “I serve Yahweh of Armies, and as surely as he lives, I would not even glance at you if it were not for Jehoshaphat, Judah’s king. I respect him.
Now someone bring me a man who plays the harp.” As the music played, Yahweh’s power came on Elisha.
He said, “Yahweh says to dig this dry valley full of pools.{d}

Yahweh tells you, ‘You will not feel any wind, and you will not see any rain. Even so, water will pour into this dry valley until it is full. Then you can drink, and so can your cattle and your other animals.’
For Yahweh, that is a small matter. He is going to put Moab in your power as well.
You will conquer each city with a wall and each fine town. You will chop down each good tree. You will stop up each spring, and you will ruin each good field by throwing rocks on it.”
The next morning, about the time the morning grain offering{e} was given, water came flowing from the direction of Edom. Soon water covered the land.
Word reached Moab that the kings were marching against them. So every man who could carry weapons, young and old, was called up. They took their places along the border.
They rose early. The sun was shining on the water, and to the Moabites across the valley it looked as red as blood.
“That is blood!” they said. “Those kings must have fought each other with swords{f} and killed one another. Come on, Moab, let’s go grab what they left!”
But when the Moabites reached Israel’s camp, the Israelites jumped up and attacked them, and the Moabites ran away. Israel’s army chased them into Moab and kept on killing them.{g}

They tore down the towns. Each soldier threw a rock onto every good field, until the fields were full of rocks. They stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree. At last only Kir-hareseth{h} was left with its stone walls. Soldiers with slings formed a ring around the city and struck at it.
The battle was going against him, and Moab’s king could see it. Taking 700 men armed with swords, he tried to cut a path through to Edom’s king. They could not do it.

So he took his oldest son, the one who was to become king after him. He offered the boy as a burnt sacrifice on top of the city wall. Then great anger{i} came against Israel. They left Moab’s king and went back to their own land.

notes.text: Mesha may mean “salvation.” His own carved stone, the Moabite Stone (about 840 B.C.), tells of Moab breaking away, from Moab’s side.
Edom means “red.” It was the land south of the Dead Sea.
The Hebrew says “What to me and to you?”
Or “trenches.” The Hebrew says “Make this valley pits, pits.”
The Hebrew says “at the going up of the minchah,” the morning grain offering.
The meaning of the Hebrew is not certain. It may mean “they have surely killed each other with the sword.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is not certain. Some ancient copies say “they went on striking.”
Kir-hareseth means “city of broken pottery” or “wall of broken pottery.” It is probably modern Kerak in Jordan.
The Hebrew word qetseph means “anger” or “fury.” It does not say whose anger it was.

verses.text: One of the prophets in Elisha’s group had died. His wife came crying to Elisha. “My husband served you,” she said, “and you know how he honored Yahweh. He left a debt behind. Now the lender wants my two boys. He says they must work for him as slaves to pay it.”
“How can I help you?” Elisha asked. “What do you have at home?” She said, “Sir, there is nothing in my house but one small jar of olive oil.”
Elisha said, “Go to all your neighbors. Ask each one to lend you empty jars. Get lots of them.
Next, take your sons inside with you and close the door tight. Pour oil from your little jar into each big one. Put each full jar off to the side.”
She left him and did it. She shut herself and her sons inside. They kept handing her jars, and she kept pouring.
Finally every jar was full. “Hand me another,” she told one son. “There aren’t any more,” he said. At that moment the oil stopped flowing.
She went back and told Elisha, God’s man. He said, “Now sell the oil and pay off what you owe. You and your sons can live on the money left over.”

One day Elisha came to Shunem.{a} A rich woman of that town invited him in and would not take no for an answer. He had to stay for a meal. From then on, whenever he traveled that way, he stopped at her house to eat.
She said to her husband, “This man who keeps coming by is a holy man. He belongs to God. I am sure of it.
Let’s build a little room with walls up on our roof for him. We can put a bed in there, with a table, a chair and a lamp. When he visits, he can use it.”
Some time later, Elisha arrived and went up to that room to lie down.
“Ask the woman from Shunem to come,” he told Gehazi,{b} his helper. Gehazi called her, and she came up to Elisha’s room.

Elisha told Gehazi, “Say to her, ‘You have taken such good care of us. What can we do for you? Should we speak to the king about you, or to the army’s commander?’” She answered, “My own family is all around me here. I am fine.”
Later Elisha talked it over with Gehazi. “Then what is there that we could do for her?” Gehazi said, “Well, she has no son. And her husband is an old man.”
“Bring her here,” Elisha said. So Gehazi called her again, and she waited in the doorway.
Elisha told her, “When this season comes around again, a son of your own will be in your arms.” “Please, sir,” she said, “you are God’s man. Do not fool me like that.”
But she became pregnant. A year later, at the very time Elisha had named, she gave birth to a son.
The boy grew older. One day he went out to his father, who was out in the fields with the workers cutting grain.
Suddenly the boy cried to his father, “My head hurts! My head!” His father told a servant, “Take him home to his mother.”
The servant lifted him up and carried him home. His mother held him on her lap until noon. Then he died.
She carried him upstairs and laid him on the bed of God’s man. She closed the door and went out.
She called out to her husband, “I need a donkey and one of the young workers. I must rush to God’s man, and I will be right back.”
“Why go today?” he asked. “It is not a new moon festival or a Sabbath.” “It will be fine,” she said.{c}
She put a saddle on the donkey. Then she told her servant, “Hurry, drive the donkey! Keep going fast unless I say to slow down.”
So she left and came to Mount Carmel, where God’s man was. Elisha saw her coming in the distance. “Look,” he told Gehazi, “it is the woman from Shunem.
Run out to her. Ask her, ‘Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is your boy all right?’” She told Gehazi, “Everything is fine.”

But when she got up the mountain to God’s man, she threw herself down and held on to his feet. Gehazi stepped in to pull her off. But God’s man said, “Leave her alone! Something has made her very sad. Yahweh has hidden it from me. He has not let me know.”
Then she spoke. “Sir, was it my idea to ask you for a son? I begged you not to fool me with hope.”{d}

Elisha told Gehazi, “Tie up your long robe so you can run. Take my walking stick and go. If someone greets you, do not greet him back. If someone says hello, do not answer. Lay my walking stick across the child’s face.”
The mother said, “I promise by Yahweh’s life, and by yours, I am not leaving without you.” So Elisha rose and went along with her.

Gehazi went on ahead. He placed the stick on the boy’s face, but the boy made no sound, and nothing showed he was alive. So Gehazi went back to meet Elisha. “The boy is still dead,” he said. “He did not wake up.”
Elisha reached the house. The boy was there, stretched out dead on Elisha’s bed.
Elisha entered and closed the door behind him. Now he and the child were alone. Then he prayed to Yahweh.
He climbed up and lay stretched out over the boy. Mouth to mouth, eye to eye, palm to palm, he covered him. As he lay there, the child’s body began to warm up.
Elisha got off the bed. He walked back and forth across the room one time. Then he climbed up again and stretched out on the boy. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Elisha called Gehazi. “Go get the woman from Shunem,” he said. So Gehazi did. When she came in, Elisha told her, “Here is your son. Take him.”
The mother came in and dropped down at Elisha’s feet with her face to the floor. Then she picked up her son and carried him out.

Elisha went back to Gilgal. There was no food in that area at that time. One day the prophets were sitting with him, and he told his servant, “Set the big pot on the fire. Cook up a stew for this group of prophets.”

One man went out into the open country looking for plants to eat. He came across a wild vine and picked its wild gourds.{e} He gathered up as many as his coat would hold. When he came back, he cut them up and dropped them into the pot. Nobody knew what they were.
They dished out the stew and handed it around. But as soon as they tasted it, they cried out, “Man of God, this pot will kill us!” They could not eat it.
“Fetch some flour,” said Elisha. He tossed it in and told them, “Now serve it to the men.” And the stew did them no harm.

A man came from Baal-shalishah.{f} He brought God’s man twenty loaves of barley bread, baked from the first grain of the harvest. He also brought a sack{g} of fresh grain. “Let the people have it,” Elisha said. “They can eat it.”
“How can this feed a hundred men?” his servant asked. But Elisha said again, “Give it to them. Yahweh says, ‘They will eat, and some will be left.’”
So the servant served the food. The men ate, and there was some left over, just as Yahweh had said.

notes.text: Shunem was in the Jezreel Valley, near modern Sulam. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
Gehazi may mean “valley of vision.”
The Hebrew says “Shalom,” meaning “peace.” The same word is in verse 26.
Or “Do not lie to me.”
This was probably colocynth, a bitter wild gourd that makes people very sick.
Baal-shalishah means “lord of Shalishah” (“the third”). It was near Gilgal in the hills of Ephraim.
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “sack” is uncertain. The Septuagint says “and cakes of figs.”

subheads.8: A Woman of Shunem Gets a Son

verses.text: Naaman{a} was in charge of the army of Aram’s king. His master thought very highly of him, because Yahweh had used Naaman to give Aram victory. He was a brave soldier, but he had a terrible skin disease.{b}
Bands of soldiers from Aram had gone on raids into Israel. One of the people they took was a young girl. Now she worked for Naaman’s wife.
One day the girl said to the woman she served, “If only my master would visit the prophet who lives in Samaria! That prophet could heal his skin.”
Naaman went to the king and told him everything the Israelite girl had said.

“Go ahead,” said Aram’s king. “I will write a letter for you to take to Israel’s king.” So Naaman set out. He took along about 750 pounds of silver,{c} about 150 pounds of gold,{d} and ten sets of fancy robes.
He brought Israel’s king the letter, which said, “The man who hands you this letter is Naaman, my servant. I have sent him so you can cure his skin disease.”

Israel’s king read it and tore his robes. “Do I have God’s power over life and death?” he cried. “This man wants me to cure someone of a skin disease! You can all see it: he is looking for an excuse to go to war.”
Elisha, God’s man, heard about the king tearing his robes. So he sent the king a message. “Why did you tear your robes?” he asked. “Have the man come to me. He will learn that Israel has a prophet.”
Naaman came with his horses and chariots. He stopped in front of the door of Elisha’s house.
Elisha did not come out. He sent someone to tell Naaman, “Go to the Jordan River and wash yourself seven times. Then your body will be made new and clean.”

That made Naaman angry, and he left. “I was sure the prophet would come out to me himself,” he said. “I thought he would stand there and pray in the name of Yahweh his God. I pictured him waving his hand over the sore spot to heal it.

Back home in Damascus we have the Abana{e} River and the Pharpar River. Aren’t they better than any water in Israel? Couldn’t I bathe in those and be made clean?” He turned around and stormed off, furious.

Naaman’s servants came up to him. “Sir,”{f} they said, “suppose the prophet had told you to do something hard. Wouldn’t you have done it? He only asked you to wash and be clean. Surely you can do that!”
So Naaman went down to the Jordan. He dipped under the water seven times, as God’s man had said. His skin became fresh and smooth, like a young boy’s. He was healed.

Then Naaman and all the people traveling with him went back to God’s man. Naaman stood before him and said, “Now I am sure of it. In all the world, there is no God except in Israel. Please, sir, let me give you a present.”{g}
Elisha answered, “I serve Yahweh. As surely as he lives, I will not take anything.” Naaman kept trying to make him take it, but Elisha would not.

“Then please do one thing for me,” Naaman said. “Let me take home as much dirt as two mules can carry.{h} From now on I will never offer a burnt offering or any sacrifice to another god. I will offer them only to Yahweh.

But there is one thing I pray Yahweh will forgive. My master goes into the temple of Rimmon{i} to worship, and I must go with him. He holds on to my arm for support, so I have to bow when he bows there. When I bow down in that temple, may Yahweh forgive me for it.”
“Go in peace,” Elisha told him. Naaman had traveled a short way{j}

when Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, God’s man, said to himself, “My master let this man from Aram off too easily. He did not take any of the gifts Naaman brought. By the life of Yahweh, I will chase him down and get some of it for myself.”
So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. Naaman looked back and saw a man running toward him. He stepped down off his chariot to greet him. “Is something wrong?” he asked.

“No, nothing is wrong,” Gehazi said. “But my master sent me with a message. Just now two young prophets came to him from the hills of Ephraim. He asks if you would give them about 75 pounds of silver{k} and two sets of clothes.”

“Of course,” said Naaman. “Please take twice that, about 150 pounds.”{l} He kept urging Gehazi. He tied the silver up in two bags, along with two sets of clothes. Two of his servants loaded up the bags and walked ahead of Gehazi with them.
When Gehazi reached the hill,{m} he took the bags from the servants. He hid them in the house and sent the men back.
Then Gehazi went in and stood before his master. “Where have you been, Gehazi?” Elisha asked. “I have not been anywhere, sir,” Gehazi said.

But Elisha said, “My spirit went with you. I was there when that man stepped off his chariot to meet you. This was no time to take silver and clothing. It was no time to get olive trees, vineyards, sheep, cattle and servants.
Because of this, the disease Naaman had will stick to you and your family line for all time.” When Gehazi walked out, his skin was diseased, white like snow.

notes.text: Naaman means “pleasant.”
The Hebrew word was traditionally translated “leprosy.” It covered many kinds of skin disease, not only the illness called leprosy today. The same is true in the rest of this chapter.
The Hebrew says “ten talents of silver.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so this was about 340 kilograms.
The Hebrew says “six thousand of gold,” probably shekels. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so this was about 69 kilograms. The Septuagint says “six thousand pieces of gold.”
The written Hebrew says Abana; the Hebrew read aloud says Amanah. Abana may mean “stony.” Pharpar may mean “swift.”
The Hebrew says “my father,” a respectful way to speak. Some read the same Hebrew letters as “if.”
The Hebrew word is berakah, “blessing.”
The Hebrew says “a load of a pair of mules.” The Septuagint adds “of the red earth.”
Rimmon was the storm god of Aram, also called Hadad-Rimmon. The name may mean “thunderer.” The Hebrew word rimmon also means “pomegranate.”
The Hebrew says “a stretch of land.” The distance is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “a talent of silver.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
The Hebrew says “two talents,” about 68 kilograms.
The Hebrew word ophel can mean “the hill” or “the fort.” The Septuagint says “a secret place.”

verses.text: One day the prophets in Elisha’s group told him, “Sir, the place where we meet with you has gotten too crowded for us.
Why don’t we go down to the Jordan? Each of us can cut a log there, and we can put up a new building to live in.” “Go ahead,” Elisha said.
One of them asked, “Won’t you please come along with us, your servants?” “Yes, I will come,” he answered.
Elisha went along. At the Jordan they started chopping trees.
One man was cutting through a log when his iron ax head flew off and dropped into the river. “Oh no, sir!” he shouted. “And I had only borrowed that ax!”{a}
“Where did it go in?” asked God’s man. The man pointed to the spot. Elisha cut a stick and tossed it there, and the iron came floating up to the top.
“Pick it up,” Elisha said. So the man reached down and took hold of it.
Once Aram’s king was at war with Israel. He made plans with his officers. “We will set up camp in this place and that place,” he told them.
But God’s man sent word to Israel’s king. “Watch out! Do not go near that place. The Arameans are on their way down there.”
So the king of Israel sent men to check the place God’s man had named. Again and again Elisha warned him. Each time the king kept guard there. It happened many times.
This made Aram’s king very upset. He called in his officers. “Who among us is a spy for Israel’s king?” he demanded. “Tell me!”
“No one, my lord and king,” one officer said. “It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel. He tells Israel’s king the very words you speak in your own bedroom.”
“Find out where this Elisha is staying,” the king ordered. “I will send men to catch him.” Someone reported, “He is staying in Dothan.”{b}
That night the king sent horses, chariots and a large fighting force. They came in the night and made a ring around the town.
The next morning Elisha’s servant got up early and went out. Soldiers with horses and chariots were all around the town! “Master, this is awful!” the servant cried. “What can we do?”
“Do not be afraid,” Elisha said. “Our side has more fighters than their side does.”
Elisha prayed, “Please, Yahweh, let my servant’s eyes be opened so he can see.” Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes. Now he saw horses and chariots of fire filling the hills all around Elisha.
The Arameans came down toward Elisha. He prayed, “Yahweh, make these people blind.”{c} And Yahweh did as Elisha asked. He struck them blind.
Elisha called to them, “You have taken the wrong road. This town is not the one you want. Follow me. I will take you to the man you are hunting for.” Then he led them all the way to Samaria.
They walked into Samaria. Then Elisha prayed, “Yahweh, open these men’s eyes now, so they can see.” Yahweh opened their eyes, and they looked around. Samaria’s walls were all around them!
Israel’s king saw them. “Father,” he asked Elisha, “should I kill them? Shall I strike them down?”

“No,” said Elisha. “You would not kill soldiers you captured in battle with your own sword and bow, would you?{d} Put bread and water before these men. When they have had their fill, send them back to the one they serve.”
So the king served them a grand meal. When they finished eating and drinking, the king let them leave, and they returned to their master. After that, raiders from Aram stayed out of Israel’s land.
Later on, Ben-hadad, Aram’s king, called up his whole army. He marched to Samaria and surrounded it to starve it out.
Food ran so short in Samaria that a donkey’s head cost about 2 pounds of silver.{e} Half a pint of dove’s dung{f} cost about 2 ounces of silver.{g}
One day the king of Israel was passing by on the wall. A woman cried up to him, “My lord the king, help me!”
He answered, “If Yahweh does not help you, how can I? I have no grain to give you from the threshing floor. I have no wine from the winepress.”
Then the king asked, “What is wrong?” She pointed to another woman. “She made a deal with me,” she said. “She said, ‘Hand over your son, and we will eat him today. Tomorrow we will eat my son.’
So we boiled my child and ate him. The next day I told her, ‘It is your turn. Give us your son to eat.’ But she has hidden her boy away.”
The king heard what she said, and he ripped his robes. He was walking on the wall, so everyone could see that he was wearing rough sackcloth under his robes, against his skin.
He said, “May God punish me, and punish me even worse, if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head before this day is over!”

Elisha was at home, and the city’s leaders sat there around him. The king sent a man on ahead. Before the messenger came, Elisha told the leaders, “Look! This son of a murderer has sent someone to chop off my head. When the man comes, shut the door. Hold it closed against him. His master is surely coming close behind. Listen for his steps.”
Elisha had not finished speaking when the messenger{h} came down to him. The king said, “Yahweh has sent this trouble on us. What is the use of waiting for Yahweh to do something?”

notes.text: The Septuagint says “and it was hidden.”
Dothan means “two wells.”
The Hebrew word is sanwerim, a rare word for a dazzling or confusing blindness (compare Genesis 19:11).
Or “Do you kill people you have captured with your sword and bow?” Even prisoners of war were not killed.
The Hebrew says “eighty of silver,” probably shekels. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so this was about 920 grams. The Septuagint says “fifty pieces of silver.”

The Hebrew says “a quarter of a kab.” A kab was about 1 1/4 quarts (1.2 liters), so this was about a third of a liter. “Dove’s dung” may be a nickname for a cheap food, such as carob pods or wild bulbs.
The Hebrew says “five of silver,” probably shekels, about 57 grams.
The Hebrew and the Septuagint say “the messenger.” Many experts read “the king,” since the king seems to speak next (compare 7:2, 17).

verses.text: Elisha said, “Listen to Yahweh’s word. Yahweh says, ‘By this time tomorrow, at Samaria’s gate, you will be able to buy 7 quarts of fine flour for about 2/5 ounce of silver. The same price will buy 14 quarts of barley.’”{a}

The king had an officer whose arm he leaned on. This officer told God’s man, “Even if Yahweh opened up windows in the sky, that could never happen!” Elisha answered, “You will see it with your own eyes. But you will not eat one bite of it.”
Just outside the city gate sat four men who had a skin disease.{b} They talked it over. “Why sit here waiting to die?” they said.

“If we go into the city, we will starve, because there is no food in there. Staying here means death too. So let’s go over to the camp of the Arameans and give ourselves up. Maybe they will let us live. Maybe they will kill us. Either way, death is coming for us anyhow.”
When it got dark, they set off for the Aramean camp. They came to the edge of it, but there was nobody there!

The Lord{c} had made the Aramean army hear a noise like chariots and horses, the sound of a huge army. The soldiers had said to each other, “Israel’s king must have hired the Hittite kings and the kings of Egypt{d} to come fight against us!”
Then, as darkness fell, they ran. Tents, horses, donkeys, everything was left behind. They abandoned the whole camp as it stood and fled to save themselves.

The four sick men came to the edge of the camp. Into a tent they went, where they had food and drink. They carried out silver, gold and clothes, and buried them out of sight. Then they came back, went into a second tent, took more things, and hid those too.

But then they had second thoughts. “We are doing wrong,” they told each other. “Today there is good news to tell, and we are silent. If we sit on it until daylight, we will be found out and punished. Let’s go right now and report it to the king’s household.”

They went to the city and called up to the gatekeepers. “We went to the Aramean camp,” they said. “Not a single person was there! We heard no one. All we saw were horses and donkeys, still tied up, and the tents left the way they were.”
The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was passed along until it reached the king’s household.

In the middle of the night, the king rose from bed. He told his officers, “I know what the Arameans are doing. They know we are starving. So they have slipped out of their tents and are hiding out in the countryside. They think, ‘When the Israelites come out of the city, we will take them alive. Then the city will be ours.’”

One of the officers suggested, “We still have a few horses in the city. Let some men ride out on five of them. If they die, they are no worse off than the rest of the Israelites here. We are all going to die like the others before us.{e} Let’s send them out and see.”
They got two chariots with horses. The king sent them to chase after the army of Aram. “Go and find out,” he ordered.

The men followed the Arameans all the way to the Jordan. Along the whole road they found clothes and equipment that the Arameans had tossed aside as they ran. The messengers came back and reported to the king.
Then the people rushed out and took everything from the Aramean camp. Now 7 quarts of fine flour cost only 2/5 ounce of silver, and so did 14 quarts of barley. It was just as Yahweh had said.

The king had put the officer who helped him walk in charge of the gate. But the people crushed him under their feet in the gateway, and he died. This was what God’s man had said when the king came to see him.
God’s man had told the king, “By this time tomorrow, at Samaria’s gate, 2/5 ounce of silver will buy 14 quarts of barley or 7 quarts of fine flour.”
And the officer had said, “Even if Yahweh made windows in the sky, this could not happen!” Elisha had replied, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it.”
It turned out just that way. The people stepped on him in the gateway, and he died.

notes.text: The Hebrew says “a seah of fine flour for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel.” A seah was about 7 quarts (about 7.3 liters). A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams). These were low prices compared with 6:25. The same is true in verses 16 and 18.
See the note at 5:1.
The Hebrew word here is Adonai.
Some experts think the Hebrew word for Egypt means Musri, a land in what is now Turkey, near the Hittite kings of northern Syria.
The Hebrew of this verse repeats itself and is somewhat uncertain.

subheads.3: Four Sick Men Find an Empty Camp

verses.text: Elisha had once spoken to the woman whose son he brought back to life. “Take your family and leave,” he told her. “Go and live anywhere you can, in another land. Yahweh has called for a famine. For seven years there will be hunger here.”
The woman did as God’s man told her. She took her family and lived among the Philistines for seven years.
When those seven years ended, she returned from Philistine country. She went to the king to beg him to give her house and land back to her.
Just then the king was speaking with Gehazi, the servant of God’s man. “I want to hear about the wonders Elisha has done,” the king said. “Tell me all of them.”

Gehazi was in the middle of telling how Elisha had raised a boy who had died. At that very moment, the boy’s mother walked in. She had come to plead with the king for her house and field. “My lord the king,” Gehazi said, “this is the woman! And this is her son, the one Elisha raised from the dead!”

The king asked her questions, and she told him all that had happened. So the king put an official in charge of her case. “Give back everything that belonged to her,” he said. “Also give her the value of all the crops her fields have grown since she went away.”
Later Elisha traveled to Damascus. At that time, Ben-hadad, who ruled Aram, lay ill. Someone told the king, “God’s man has come here.”
Ben-hadad told Hazael, “Take a gift and go see God’s man. Have him ask Yahweh whether I will get well from this sickness.”

Hazael went to meet Elisha. He brought a gift of the best things Damascus had to offer, loaded on forty camels. He came and stood before Elisha. “Your son Ben-hadad, Aram’s king, has sent me,” he said. “He wants to know, ‘Will I get over this sickness?’”
Elisha answered, “Go tell him,{a} ‘You will surely get well.’ Yet Yahweh has let me see that death is coming for him.”
Elisha kept staring at Hazael until Hazael felt uneasy.{b} Then God’s man began to cry.

“Sir, what makes you weep?” Hazael asked. Elisha said, “I can see the evil you will bring on Israel’s people. Their forts will go up in flames by your hand. Their young men will fall by your swords. You will dash their little ones to pieces and slit open their women who carry babies.”
Hazael said, “How could someone like me, no better than a dog, do such great things?” Elisha said, “Yahweh has let me see you as Aram’s king.”
Then Hazael went back to Ben-hadad. “What did Elisha tell you?” his master asked. “He told me you would surely get well,” said Hazael.
But the next day Hazael took a thick cloth and soaked it in water. Then he pressed it down over Ben-hadad’s face, and the king died. Then Hazael became king in his place.
Joram son of Ahab was in his fifth year as Israel’s king. Jehoshaphat had been king of Judah.{c} Then Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram began to rule Judah.
Jehoram was crowned at age 32. For eight years he ruled from Jerusalem.
Like the kings of Israel, and like Ahab’s family, he went the wrong way, because Ahab’s daughter was his wife. Jehoram did what Yahweh saw as evil.
But because of David, his servant, Yahweh did not want to destroy Judah. He had promised that a lamp would always burn for David and his children after him.
While Jehoram was king, Edom broke free from Judah and chose its own king.

So Joram took all his chariots and went over to Zair.{d} The Edomites had surrounded him and his chariot leaders. In the dark he rose and broke through their lines. But his soldiers scattered and fled home.{e}
Edom has been free from Judah’s rule from then until now. Libnah{f} broke away from Judah at that same time too.
Everything else Joram did is written in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Joram died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in David’s City. His son Ahaziah became king after him.
Ahaziah son of Jehoram started to rule Judah in the twelfth year that Joram son of Ahab ruled Israel.
Ahaziah was 22 when he took the throne, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted one year. Athaliah,{g} a granddaughter{h} of Omri, king of Israel, was his mother.
Ahaziah copied the ways of Ahab’s family. Like them, he did what Yahweh saw as evil, because he was related to them by marriage.
Together with Ahab’s son Joram, Ahaziah marched to Ramoth-gilead to battle against Hazael, king of Aram. There the Arameans wounded Joram.

So King Joram went back to Jezreel to heal. He had been hurt by the Arameans at Ramah{i} while fighting Hazael, Aram’s king. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, Judah’s king, went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, who was hurt.

notes.text: The Hebrew read aloud and many ancient copies say “Go tell him.” The written Hebrew says “Go and say, ‘You will surely not get well.’”
It is not clear who is doing what. Either Elisha stared at Hazael until Hazael was embarrassed, or the other way around.
The words “Jehoshaphat had been king of Judah” are in both the Hebrew and the Septuagint, but many experts think they were copied by accident from the end of the verse.
No one knows where Zair was. 2 Chronicles 21:9 does not name it.
The Hebrew of this verse is hard to understand, and it is unclear how the battle ended.
Libnah means “whiteness.” It was a town in the low hills of Judah.
Athaliah may mean “Yahweh is lifted up.”
The Hebrew says “daughter,” meaning a female descendant. She was Ahab’s daughter (verse 18).
That is, Ramoth-gilead.

subheads.1: The Shunammite Gets Her Land Back

verses.text: Elisha the prophet called over a young man from the group of prophets. “Tie up your robe for travel,” he told him. “Carry this little jar of olive oil and hurry to Ramoth-gilead.
Once there, find Jehu,{a} whose father was Jehoshaphat and whose grandfather was Nimshi. Call him away from the men he is with and take him to a back room.
Pour the oil over his head. Tell him, ‘Yahweh says this: I am making you king of Israel by pouring oil on you.’ Then get out the door and run. Waste no time.”
So the young prophet set off for Ramoth-gilead.
He found the army’s leaders sitting together in a meeting. “Commander, I have word to give you,” he said. Jehu asked, “Which of us do you mean?” “You, sir,” the young man said.

Jehu rose and stepped indoors. There the prophet emptied the jar of oil over his head. Then he said, “Israel’s God, Yahweh, says this: ‘I am pouring oil on you to make you king of Yahweh’s people Israel.

It is your task to wipe out the family of Ahab, the master you served. Through you I will punish Jezebel. She murdered my servants, the prophets, and many others who served Yahweh, and I will make her pay for their blood.
Ahab’s whole family line will come to an end. I will remove every male in Ahab’s family in Israel, slave or free.{b}
I will deal with Ahab’s family the way I dealt with Jeroboam’s family. Jeroboam was Nebat’s son. I will treat it the way I treated the family of Baasha son of Ahijah.
And Jezebel’s body will be food for dogs on the land at Jezreel, and she will have no grave.’” With that, the young prophet threw open the door and fled.

Jehu stepped back out to where the other officers sat. “Is everything all right?” one of them asked. “Why did that madman come to see you?” Jehu said, “You know his type, and you know how such men talk.”
“You are not telling us the truth,” they said. “Tell us what he said.” Jehu answered, “He told me this and this. He said, ‘Yahweh says: I am pouring oil on you to make you king of Israel.’”
Right away each officer pulled off his coat and spread it under Jehu’s feet on the steps.{c} They blew a trumpet and cheered, “Jehu is king!”
So Jehu, Nimshi’s grandson and Jehoshaphat’s son, made plans to overthrow Joram. At that time, Joram and the army of Israel had been guarding Ramoth-gilead from Hazael, king of Aram.

But King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to heal from wounds he got in his battle with Hazael, Aram’s king. Jehu told the officers, “If you agree with me, do not let anyone sneak out of the city. No one must get to Jezreel to warn them.”
Then Jehu climbed into his chariot and set off for Jezreel. Joram was lying there wounded, and King Ahaziah of Judah had come down to see him.

Up on Jezreel’s tower a lookout was keeping watch. He spotted Jehu and his soldiers coming. “I see a crowd of soldiers!” he called. “Get a rider,” Joram ordered. “Send him out to meet them. He must find out if they are friends or enemies.”

The rider went out to meet Jehu. “The king asks whether this is a peaceful visit,” he said. “What does peace matter to you?” Jehu answered. “Turn and ride behind me.” The watchman called out, “The rider got to them, but he is not on his way back.”
So the king sent out a second rider. He reached them and said, “The king asks, ‘Is it peace?’” Jehu said, “Why do you care about peace? Come fall in behind me.”
The watchman reported again, “He reached them too, and he is not coming back either. And the man in that chariot must be Jehu son of Nimshi. He drives like a wild man!”

“Get my chariot ready,” Joram commanded. When the horses were hitched, the two kings set out, Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, riding side by side in separate chariots. They came face to face with Jehu on the land that had once been owned by Naboth from Jezreel.
Joram saw Jehu and called out, “Do you come in peace, Jehu?” Jehu shouted back, “How can there be peace while your mother Jezebel goes on worshiping idols and doing all her witchcraft?”
Joram swung his chariot around{d} and raced off. “It is a trap, Ahaziah!” he yelled.
Jehu pulled back his bow as hard as he could. His arrow struck Joram in the back, between his shoulders, and went through his heart. Joram dropped down dead in his chariot.

Jehu told his officer Bidkar, “Pick up his body and throw it on the field that belonged to Naboth from Jezreel. You and I once rode together behind Ahab, this man’s father. Do you remember that? Back then Yahweh spoke this message{e} against him:

‘Yesterday I saw Naboth’s blood and the blood of his sons. That is what Yahweh says. On this very field I will make you pay for it. That is Yahweh’s promise.’ So now, pick Joram up and toss him onto that field. That is what Yahweh said would happen.”

Ahaziah, Judah’s king, saw what happened and ran off along the road to Beth-haggan.{f} Jehu raced after him. “Kill him too!” he shouted. They shot him{g} as he rode in his chariot up the hill toward Gur, near Ibleam. He got as far as Megiddo and died there.
His servants laid Ahaziah’s body in a chariot and drove it home to Jerusalem. They buried him in his own grave beside his ancestors in David’s City.
In Joram’s eleventh{h} year as Israel’s king, Ahaziah had begun to rule Judah.
Next Jehu came to Jezreel. Jezebel heard he was coming. She painted around her eyes,{i} fixed her hair, and looked out from an upstairs window.
Jehu rode in through the gate, and she shouted down, “Is this a peaceful visit, you Zimri? You murdered your master!”{j}
Jehu looked up at her window. “Who is with me?” he called. “Anyone?” Two or three palace officials leaned out and looked down at him.
“Toss her out!” Jehu ordered. They threw her down. Her blood splashed onto the wall and onto the horses, and Jehu’s horses ran over her.
Jehu went inside and had a meal. Then he said, “Take care of that cursed woman. Bury her. After all, a king’s daughter is what she was.”
But when they went out to bury her, almost nothing was left. A skull, two feet and the palms of her hands were all they could find.
They returned and told Jehu. He said, “Yahweh spoke this through his servant Elijah from Tishbe: ‘On the land at Jezreel, dogs will eat Jezebel’s flesh.
Her body will lie on the ground at Jezreel like manure scattered on a field. Nobody will look at it and know it was Jezebel.’”

notes.text: Jehu means “Yahweh is he.”
The Hebrew words are hard to translate. See the note at 1 Kings 14:10.
The meaning of the Hebrew words for “on the steps” is uncertain. It may mean “at the top of the stairs.”
The Hebrew says “turned his hands,” meaning he turned the chariot around by its reins.
The Hebrew word is massa, “burden,” a word used for a serious message from a prophet.
Beth-haggan means “house of the garden.” It is probably modern Jenin.
The Septuagint and some other ancient copies say “They shot him.” The Hebrew does not have these words.
8:25 says the twelfth year. The two numbers come from different ways of counting years, and both are left as they are.
The Hebrew says “set her eyes in antimony,” a dark eye paint.
Zimri killed his master, King Elah, and ruled for only seven days (1 Kings 16:9-18).

verses.text: There were seventy sons of Ahab living in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria. They were addressed to the leaders of Jezreel,{a} to the elders, and to the men who were raising Ahab’s sons. The letters said,
“Your master’s sons are there with you. You also have chariots and horses, a city with strong walls, and weapons. So the moment you get this letter,
choose the best and most able of your master’s sons. Make him king in his father’s place. Then fight to defend your master’s family.”
But the men in Samaria were scared to death. “Jehu has beaten two kings already,” they said. “What hope do we have?”

So the man in charge of the palace, the city’s governor, the elders and the men raising the boys sent Jehu a reply. “We are your servants,” they said. “Whatever you command, we will do. None of the princes will be crowned by us. The choice is yours.”

Jehu wrote them another letter. “If you are on my side and will obey me,” he said, “then cut off the heads of your master’s sons. Bring them to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” The seventy princes were in the homes of the city’s chief men, who were bringing them up.
When the letter came, the leaders took the seventy princes and killed every one. They packed the heads in baskets and had them carried to Jezreel for Jehu.
A messenger came to Jehu. “They have brought the princes’ heads,” he reported. Jehu said, “Make two heaps of them at the entrance of the gate. Leave them there until morning.”
At sunrise Jehu came out and stood before the whole crowd. “You are not guilty,” he said. “It was I who plotted against my master and took his life. But who struck down all these men?
So understand this: every word Yahweh spoke against Ahab’s family will come true. Not one will fail. Yahweh has done what he promised through his servant Elijah.”
Then Jehu killed everyone in Jezreel still left from Ahab’s family. He also killed Ahab’s important officials, his close friends and his priests. Not one of them lived.
Then Jehu left Jezreel and headed toward Samaria. Along the road was Beth-eked of the Shepherds.{b}

At that spot Jehu came upon some relatives of Ahaziah, Judah’s king. He asked them, “Who might you be?” “We are relatives of Ahaziah,” they said. “We are traveling down to greet the royal family, the sons of the king and of the queen mother.”
“Seize them, but do not kill them yet!” Jehu ordered. His men grabbed them and killed them beside the well at Beth-eked, forty-two men in all. Jehu did not let even one of them live.

Jehu went on from there. Along the way he met Jehonadab{c} son of Rechab, who was coming to meet him. Jehu greeted him and asked, “Is your heart loyal to me, the way mine is loyal to you?” “It is,” said Jehonadab. Jehu said,{d} “Then reach out your hand to me.” Jehonadab did, and Jehu pulled him up to ride beside him.
“Come along,” Jehu said. “Watch how strongly I stand up for Yahweh.” So Jehonadab rode along with him.
Jehu reached Samaria. There he killed all who were left of Ahab’s family, until none remained. This was what Yahweh had said through Elijah.
Then Jehu called all the people together. “Ahab served Baal some,” he told them. “But Jehu is going to serve him much more.

Now bring me all of Baal’s prophets, all his worshipers and all his priests. Make sure not one of them is missing. I am planning a huge sacrifice in Baal’s honor. If anyone stays away, he will die for it.” But it was a trick. Jehu planned to wipe out all who worshiped Baal.
“Call a holy meeting to honor Baal,” Jehu commanded. So the announcement went out.
Jehu sent messengers through all of Israel. Every worshiper of Baal came. No one stayed home. They crowded into Baal’s temple until it was packed from wall to wall.
Jehu told the man in charge of the robes, “Get robes for everyone who worships Baal.” So the man handed out robes to them all.

Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab then entered the temple of Baal. He told Baal’s worshipers, “Look around and be sure that no one who worships Yahweh is here. Only people who worship Baal may be in this place.”

Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Outside, Jehu had placed eighty of his men with these orders: “I am putting these people into your hands. If even one of them gets away, the man who lets him escape will die in his place.”

Jehu finished offering the burnt offering. Then he told the guards and officers, “Go in and kill them! Let no one get out.” So they cut them down with swords and threw the bodies out. Then the guards and officers went into the inner room{e} of Baal’s temple.
They dragged out the holy pillar{f} from Baal’s temple and burned it.
They broke down Baal’s stone pillar and wrecked his temple. They turned the building into a toilet for the public, and it has stayed that way to this day.{g}
That is how Jehu removed Baal worship from Israel.
But Jehu did not stop the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had brought on Israel. He let the golden calves at Bethel and Dan remain.
Yahweh told Jehu, “You have done well. You did what I see as right, and you did to Ahab’s family all that I wanted done. So your sons will rule Israel after you, down to your great-great-grandsons.”
But Jehu did not carefully obey the Law of Yahweh, Israel’s God, with all his heart. He did not give up the sins of Jeroboam, which had led Israel into sin.
At that time Yahweh began to cut away parts of Israel.{h} Hazael beat the Israelites everywhere along their borders.
He took the land east of the Jordan, all of Gilead, where the tribes of Gad, Reuben and Manasseh lived. He took everything from Aroer near the Arnon Valley, both Gilead and Bashan.
The other things Jehu did, all his deeds and all his power, are recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings.
Then Jehu died and was laid to rest with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz{i} took his place as king.
In all, Jehu was Israel’s king for twenty-eight years, ruling from Samaria.

notes.text: The Hebrew says “Jezreel.” The Septuagint says “Samaria.” Some experts suggest “the city.”
Or “the shearing house of the shepherds.” Beth-eked means “house of tying,” perhaps a place where sheep were tied for shearing.
Jehonadab means “Yahweh is generous.” His family, the Rechabites, appear in Jeremiah 35.
The Septuagint has “Jehu said.” The Hebrew does not.
The Hebrew says “to the city of the house of Baal.” The meaning is uncertain. It may be the inner holy room or a fortress.
The Septuagint and some other ancient copies say “pillar.” The Hebrew says “pillars” but then “burned it.”
The Hebrew read aloud has this word. The written Hebrew has a cruder word for the same thing.
Or “to make Israel smaller.”
Jehoahaz means “Yahweh has grasped.”

subheads.18: Jehu Destroys the Worship of Baal

verses.text: Athaliah was Ahaziah’s mother. When she learned that her son was dead, she started killing off the whole royal family.

But Jehosheba{a} saved one boy. Her father was King Joram, and Ahaziah was her brother. She took Ahaziah’s son Joash{b} and slipped him away from the other princes who were about to be killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom where Athaliah could not find them. So Joash was not murdered.
For six years he stayed hidden with Jehosheba at Yahweh’s temple. During those years, the country was under Athaliah’s rule.

When the seventh year came, Jehoiada{c} called for the leaders of the Carites{d} and the palace guards, men who each led a hundred soldiers. He brought them to Yahweh’s temple. There he made an agreement with them and had them take an oath. After that, he let them see the young prince.
Then he told them his plan. “Listen carefully,” he said. “Those of you who start your work on the Sabbath will split into three groups. One group will stand guard at the palace.
The next group will watch the Sur Gate. The last group will be at the gate behind the guards. In this way you will guard the palace in shifts.{e}
The two groups of you who go off duty on the Sabbath will guard Yahweh’s temple to protect the king.
Form a circle around the young king, each man with his weapons ready. Kill anyone who tries to get through your lines. Stay right beside the king wherever he goes.”
The leaders carried out all that Jehoiada the priest commanded. They came to him with their men, both the group starting work on the Sabbath and the group ending work that day.
Then the priest gave the commanders the spears and small shields that had belonged to King David. They had been stored in Yahweh’s temple.
Each guard stood at his post, weapon in hand. They made a wall of men around the king. It stretched across the front of the temple from one side to the other, by the altar and by the temple.

Then Jehoiada brought out the king’s son. He placed the crown on the boy’s head and handed him a copy of God’s agreement.{f} They declared him king and poured oil on him. The people clapped their hands and cheered, “Long live the king!”
Athaliah could hear the shouting of the guards and the crowd. She went out to the crowd at Yahweh’s temple.

There she saw the young king standing next to the pillar, as kings did at such times. The officers and trumpet players were beside him. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Athaliah tore her robes. “Traitors!” she screamed. “Traitors!”

Jehoiada the priest spoke to the commanders who led the troops. “March her out between your rows of men,” he said. “Kill anyone who follows her.” He had told them, “Do not put her to death inside Yahweh’s temple.”
So they took hold of her and led her out by the path where horses enter the palace grounds. That is where she was killed.
Jehoiada then had the king and the people make a solemn promise to Yahweh. They agreed they would belong to Yahweh as his people. The king and the people made promises to each other as well.

All the people of the land went to Baal’s temple and pulled it down. They broke up his altars and smashed his idols. They killed Mattan, Baal’s priest, in front of the altars. Then Jehoiada the priest put guards in charge of Yahweh’s temple.

He took with him the commanders, the Carites, the guards and all the people of the land. Together they brought the king down from Yahweh’s temple. They went in through the Gate of the Guards to the palace. The boy took his seat on the king’s throne.
Everyone in the land celebrated. The city was quiet now, because Athaliah had been killed with the sword at the palace.
Jehoash{g} was only seven when he began to rule.

notes.text: Jehosheba means “Yahweh is an oath.” 2 Chronicles 22:11 calls her Jehoshabeath and says she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.
Joash, also spelled Jehoash (verse 21), means “Yahweh has given.”
Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.”
The Carites were probably hired foreign soldiers, perhaps from Caria in what is now Turkey.
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “take turns” is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is eduth. It was probably a written copy of the agreement law (compare Deuteronomy 17:18).
This is 12:1 in Hebrew. The Hebrew verse numbers in chapter 12 are one higher than the English.

verses.text: Jehoash began his reign in Jehu’s seventh year as Israel’s king. Jehoash ruled from Jerusalem for forty years. Zibiah{a} from Beersheba was his mother.
All his life Jehoash did what pleased Yahweh, since Jehoiada the priest was there to teach him.{b}
But the hilltop shrines stayed in use. People went on offering sacrifices and burning incense at them.

Jehoash gave the priests an order. “Money is brought to Yahweh’s temple as holy gifts,” he said. “There is money people pay when they are counted,{c} money paid to keep a vow, and money people give from the heart because they want to.
Let each priest collect that money from the people he deals with.{d} Then use it to fix the temple wherever repairs are needed.”
But twenty-three years into the rule of King Jehoash, the priests had still not fixed the temple.

So King Jehoash called in Jehoiada the priest and the other priests. “Why are the temple repairs not done?” he asked. “From now on, do not keep the money from the people you deal with. Turn it over to pay for fixing the temple.”
The priests agreed. They would collect no more money from the people. The repair work would not be their job anymore.

Jehoiada the priest found a wooden chest and bored a hole through its lid. He set it beside the altar, to the right of the way in to Yahweh’s temple. Every gift brought to the temple was dropped into the chest by the priests who kept watch at the door.
Whenever they saw that the chest was full of money, the king’s secretary and the high priest came. They tied up{e} the money from Yahweh’s temple in bags and counted it.
Once they had weighed it, they handed it to the men who were overseeing the work at the temple. Those men paid it out to the woodworkers and builders working on Yahweh’s temple.
They also paid the men who laid stone and the men who cut it. They bought wood and cut stone to repair Yahweh’s temple, and paid every other cost of fixing it.
None of the money that came into Yahweh’s temple was used to make things for it. No silver bowls, wick trimmers, basins or trumpets were made, and nothing else of gold or silver.
All the money went to the workers, and they used it to repair Yahweh’s temple.
No one asked the overseers to report how they spent the money they gave the workers. Those men could be trusted.
The money paid for guilt offerings and sin offerings did not go to Yahweh’s temple. It belonged to the priests.
Around this time Hazael, Aram’s king, went to war against Gath and conquered it. Next he set his sights on Jerusalem and started toward it.

So Jehoash, Judah’s king, gathered up the holy gifts given to Yahweh by the kings before him, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram and Ahaziah, along with his own. He took all the gold he could find in the storerooms of Yahweh’s temple and of the palace. All of it went as a payment to Hazael. So Aram’s king turned back from Jerusalem.
Everything else that Joash did is written in the official history of Judah’s kings.
His own officials made a secret plan against Joash. They murdered him at Beth-millo,{f} along the road down to Silla.{g}
The men who struck him down were his officials Jozacar{h} son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer. Joash was buried in David’s City beside his ancestors. Amaziah,{i} his son, ruled after him.

notes.text: Zibiah means “gazelle.” The verse numbers in this chapter follow the English. The Hebrew numbers are one higher.
Or “All the days that Jehoiada the priest taught him, Jehoash did what pleased Yahweh.” Compare 2 Chronicles 24:2, 17-22.
The meaning of the Hebrew is not clear. It may refer to the tax paid when people were counted (Exodus 30:13), or to money in common use.
The meaning of the Hebrew word makkar is uncertain. It may mean a friend, a giver or a tax official. The Septuagint says “from his sale.” The same word is in verse 7.
Or “melted down,” as some experts read it.
Beth-millo means “house of the Millo.” It was probably a building on the raised land in Jerusalem (compare 1 Kings 9:15).
No one knows where Silla was. The Septuagint says “Sela.”
Jozacar means “Yahweh has remembered.” The Septuagint says “Jezirchar.” 2 Chronicles 24:26 names the men Zabad and Jehozabad.
Amaziah means “Yahweh is strong.”

verses.text: Joash son of Ahaziah had ruled Judah for twenty-three years when Jehu’s son Jehoahaz took the throne of Israel in Samaria. His reign lasted seventeen years.
Jehoahaz did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. He kept on with the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had taught Israel. He never let go of them.
That made Yahweh very angry with Israel. All through those years he let Hazael, king of Aram, and Hazael’s son Ben-hadad defeat them again and again.
Then Jehoahaz begged Yahweh for help. Yahweh heard him, because he saw how hard Aram’s king was crushing Israel.
So Yahweh sent Israel someone to rescue them,{a} and they got free from Aram’s power. Then the Israelites could live safely at home{b} as they once had.
Yet they kept on with the sins Jeroboam’s family had led Israel into. They did not stop. The Asherah pole{c} was left standing in Samaria too.
Of Jehoahaz’s army only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and 10,000 foot soldiers were left. Aram’s king had destroyed the rest. He had crushed them like dust stamped on the ground where grain is beaten.
The other things Jehoahaz did, all his deeds and his power, are recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings.
When Jehoahaz died, he was laid to rest with his ancestors in Samaria. Joash his son ruled after him.
In the thirty-seventh year that Joash ruled Judah, a son of Jehoahaz called Jehoash became Israel’s king in Samaria. He ruled sixteen years.
Jehoash did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into sin, and Jehoash kept on doing all the same sins.
The other things Joash did, including his battles against Amaziah, Judah’s king, and all his power, are recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings.
Joash died and joined his ancestors, and Jeroboam{d} sat on his throne after him. Joash was buried in Samaria, in the tombs of Israel’s kings.
Elisha became sick with the illness that would end his life. Joash, Israel’s king, came down to see him. He cried over him. “My father! My father!” he wept. “You were Israel’s chariots and horsemen!”
“Get a bow and some arrows,” Elisha told him. So the king got them.
“Put your hand on the bow,” Elisha said to Israel’s king. When the king held it, Elisha placed his own hands over the king’s hands.

“Now open the window that faces east,” Elisha said. When it was open, Elisha said, “Shoot!” So Joash let an arrow fly. Elisha said, “That is Yahweh’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram! You will fight the Arameans at Aphek until you wipe them out.”
Next Elisha said, “Take the arrows.” The king took them. “Hit the ground with them,” Elisha told him. Three times the king beat the ground. Then he stopped.
God’s man was angry with him. “Five or six blows were needed!” he said. “Then Aram would have been beaten by you until nothing was left of it. As it is, you will win against Aram just three times.”
Then Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of raiders from Moab used to invade the land every spring.{e}

Once, while a funeral was taking place, the mourners caught sight of a raiding band. In a hurry they tossed the dead man into the tomb where Elisha lay. The body touched Elisha’s bones, and at once the man lived again and rose to his feet!
King Hazael of Aram made life hard for Israel as long as Jehoahaz lived.

But Yahweh was kind to the Israelites. He felt sorry for them and cared for them. Long ago he had made a promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he kept it in mind. He did not want to destroy them, and he has not sent them away from his presence even now.
When Aram’s king Hazael died, Ben-hadad his son took over the throne.

Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back towns from Ben-hadad son of Hazael. Hazael had captured those towns from his father Jehoahaz in war. Three times Joash beat Ben-hadad, and he won back Israel’s towns.

notes.text: The rescuer is not named. He may be Jeroboam II (14:27), or an Assyrian king who attacked Aram from the north.
The Hebrew says “in their tents.”
The Hebrew word is asherah, a wooden pole or image of the goddess Asherah.
This is Jeroboam II (14:23-29). Jeroboam probably means “may the people grow in number.”
The Hebrew says “at the coming of the year,” meaning in spring, the season for war (compare 1 Kings 20:22, 26).

subheads.20: A Dead Man Comes Back to Life

verses.text: Amaziah son of Joash started to rule Judah when Joash son of Joahaz was in his second year as Israel’s king.
Amaziah was crowned at twenty-five. For twenty-nine years he reigned in Jerusalem. Jehoaddin{a} from Jerusalem was his mother.
Amaziah did what pleased Yahweh, though he did not match his ancestor David. He followed his father Joash’s example in every way.
But the hilltop shrines stayed in use. People went on offering sacrifices and burning incense at them.
As soon as his power as king was firm, Amaziah executed the officials who had murdered his father, the king.

The murderers’ sons, though, he let live. In this he kept the rule in the Book of the Law of Moses. There Yahweh commanded, “Parents must not die for what their children do. Children must not die for what their parents do. Each one dies for his own sin.”{b}
Amaziah defeated 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He took Sela{c} in battle and gave it a new name, Joktheel.{d} That is still its name now.
Then Amaziah sent a challenge to Jehoash, the ruler of Israel. (Jehoash was Jehoahaz’s son and Jehu’s grandson.) “Come out,” he dared him. “Let us meet face to face in battle.”

Jehoash answered Amaziah with a story. “There was a thornbush up in Lebanon,” he said. “It sent a message to a tall cedar there: ‘Give my son your daughter for a wife.’ Then a wild beast of Lebanon walked over the thornbush and crushed it flat.
It is true that you beat Edom. Now you think you are great. Enjoy your fame, then, but do it at home! Why ask for trouble? It will bring you down, and Judah too.”
Amaziah paid no attention. So King Jehoash of Israel marched out. He and King Amaziah of Judah met in battle at Beth-shemesh,{e} a town in Judah.
Judah was beaten by Israel, and the men of Judah all ran home.{f}

King Jehoash of Israel took King Amaziah of Judah prisoner there at Beth-shemesh. (Amaziah’s father was Jehoash, and his grandfather was Ahaziah.) Then Jehoash went to Jerusalem. He tore down about 600 feet{g} of the city wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.

Every bit of gold and silver, and every valuable object in Yahweh’s temple and the palace storerooms, he took away. He also took people as prisoners to make sure Judah kept the peace. Then he went back to Samaria.
Everything else Jehoash did, his power and his war with Amaziah, Judah’s king, is written down in the official history of Israel’s kings.
Jehoash was laid to rest with his ancestors and buried among Israel’s kings in Samaria. His son Jeroboam then ruled.
Amaziah son of Joash, Judah’s king, lived on for fifteen years after Israel’s King Jehoash son of Jehoahaz had died.
The other things Amaziah did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Some people in Jerusalem made a plot against Amaziah. He escaped to Lachish, but they hunted him down and killed him there.
His body was brought back on horses. He was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem, in David’s City.
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah,{h} who was sixteen, and made him king to replace his father Amaziah.
After his father died and joined his ancestors, Azariah rebuilt Elath{i} and won it back for Judah.
Jeroboam son of Joash became Israel’s king in Samaria in the fifteenth year that Amaziah son of Joash ruled Judah. Jeroboam was king for forty-one years.
Jeroboam did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into sin, and this Jeroboam never gave up any of those sins.

He won back land for Israel all the way from Lebo-hamath{j} at its north end down to the Sea of the Arabah.{k} Yahweh, Israel’s God, had said this would happen. He had spoken it through his servant Jonah{l} son of Amittai, a prophet from Gath-hepher.{m}
Yahweh had seen how bitterly the Israelites were suffering, slaves and free people alike.{n} No one was left to help Israel.
But Yahweh had never said he would erase Israel’s name from under the sky. Instead he rescued them through Jeroboam son of Joash.

The other things Jeroboam did, his deeds, his power and his wars, are recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings. It tells how he won back Damascus and Hamath, which had once belonged to Judah.{o}
Jeroboam rested with his ancestors, Israel’s kings. Zechariah,{p} his son, took the throne.

notes.text: The written Hebrew says Jehoaddin. The Hebrew read aloud and 2 Chronicles 25:1 say “Jehoaddan.” The name may mean “Yahweh is delight.”
Deuteronomy 24:16.
Sela means “rock.” It was a fortress of Edom.
Joktheel may mean “God destroys” or “God feeds.” The meaning is uncertain.
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.”
The Hebrew says “to his tent.”
The Hebrew says “four hundred cubits.” A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), so this was about 180 meters.
Azariah means “Yahweh has helped.” He is also called Uzziah (15:13; 2 Chronicles 26:1).
Elath, at the top of the Gulf of Aqaba, means “large trees” or “palms.”
Or “the entrance of Hamath,” at the northern border.
That is, the Dead Sea.
Jonah means “dove.” He is the prophet in the book of Jonah.
Gath-hepher means “winepress of the well.” It was a town in Zebulun.
The Hebrew words are hard to translate. See the note at 1 Kings 14:10.
The Hebrew here says “to Judah in Israel.” Its meaning is unclear.
Zechariah means “Yahweh has remembered.”

verses.text: When Jeroboam had been Israel’s king for twenty-seven years, Amaziah’s son Azariah began to rule Judah.
Azariah was only sixteen at his crowning, and his reign in Jerusalem went on for fifty-two years. Jecoliah{a} from Jerusalem was his mother.
Azariah did what pleased Yahweh, the same as his father Amaziah had done in every way.
But the hilltop shrines stayed in use. People went on offering sacrifices and burning incense at them.

Yahweh struck the king with a skin disease{b} that stayed with him until his death. He had to live apart in a house of his own.{c} His son Jotham{d} ran the palace and governed the people of the land.
The other things Azariah did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
When Azariah died, they laid him in a grave close to his ancestors in David’s City. Jotham, his son, then ruled.
Zechariah son of Jeroboam ruled Israel from Samaria for just six months. He became king in Azariah’s thirty-eighth year as Judah’s king.
Like his ancestors, Zechariah did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into sin, and Zechariah held on to those sins.
Shallum son of Jabesh made a plot against Zechariah. In front of the people{e} he attacked and killed him. Then Shallum made himself king.
The other things Zechariah did are written in the official history of Israel’s kings.
This is how Yahweh’s word to Jehu came true. He had said, “Four generations of your sons will sit on Israel’s throne.” Things turned out exactly that way.
Uzziah{f} was in his thirty-ninth year as Judah’s king when Shallum son of Jabesh took Israel’s throne. He was king in Samaria for one month only.
Then Menahem{g} son of Gadi came up to Samaria from Tirzah. He struck down Shallum, Jabesh’s son, and took his life. Then Menahem took over as king.
The other things Shallum did, including his plot, are written in the official history of Israel’s kings.

At that time Menahem went out from Tirzah and attacked Tiphsah{h} and the land around it. He struck everyone in the town, because they had refused to open their gates to him. He destroyed the town, and he cut open every woman there who was expecting a baby.
Menahem son of Gadi took Israel’s throne in Azariah’s thirty-ninth year as king of Judah. From Samaria Menahem ruled for ten years.
Menahem did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. His whole life long, he clung to the wrongs that Nebat’s son Jeroboam had brought into Israel.
Then Pul,{i} king of Assyria, invaded the land. Menahem paid Pul about 37 tons of silver{j} to win his support and make his own hold on the kingdom stronger.
Menahem got the money by making every rich man in Israel pay about 20 ounces of silver.{k} He gave it to Assyria’s king. So the Assyrian king went home and did not stay in Israel.
The other things Menahem did are recorded in the official history of Israel’s kings.
Menahem rested with his ancestors. His son Pekahiah{l} took his place as king.
Pekahiah son of Menahem took Israel’s throne in Samaria in the fiftieth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah. Pekahiah ruled two years.
Pekahiah did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. The sins started by Jeroboam son of Nebat went on under him too, and Israel kept sinning.

Pekah{m} son of Remaliah, one of Pekahiah’s army officers, plotted against the king. Pekah took fifty men from Gilead with him. They killed Pekahiah in the strongest part of the palace at Samaria. Argob and Arieh{n} were killed along with him. Then Pekah made himself king.
The other things Pekahiah did are written in the official history of Israel’s kings.
In Azariah’s fifty-second year as Judah’s king, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel in Samaria. His rule lasted twenty years.
Pekah did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. Like the kings before him, he held to the false worship Jeroboam son of Nebat had set up for Israel.

While Pekah was Israel’s king, Tiglath-pileser,{o} king of Assyria, invaded. One by one he captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah and Janoah, then Kedesh and Hazor. He captured the regions of Gilead and Galilee, the whole land of Naphtali. He took the people away as captives to Assyria.
Then Hoshea{p} son of Elah made a secret plan to get rid of Pekah. He attacked and killed him and became king in his place. This was in Jotham son of Uzziah’s twentieth year.
The other things Pekah did are written in the official history of Israel’s kings.
Pekah son of Remaliah was in his second year as Israel’s king when Jotham son of Uzziah began to rule Judah.
At twenty-five Jotham took the throne, and for sixteen years he ruled from Jerusalem. Jerusha, Zadok’s daughter, was his mother.
Jotham did what pleased Yahweh. He lived the way his father Uzziah had lived.
But the hilltop shrines stayed in use. People went on offering sacrifices and burning incense at them. Jotham built the Upper Gate of Yahweh’s temple.
The other things Jotham did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
