In those days Yahweh began to send Rezin,{q} king of Aram, and Remaliah’s son Pekah to make war on Judah.
When Jotham died, he was laid in the family tombs in the city of his ancestor David. Then his son Ahaz{r} became king.

notes.text: Jecoliah means “Yahweh is able.”
See the note at 5:1.
The Hebrew words may mean “a house of freedom,” that is, free from the work of a king. The exact meaning is uncertain.
Jotham means “Yahweh is perfect.”
The Hebrew words for “in front of the people” are unusual. The Septuagint says “in Keblaam,” which some think means Ibleam (compare 9:27).
Uzziah is another name for Azariah. It means “Yahweh is my strength.”
Menahem means “comforter.”
The Hebrew says Tiphsah. Tiphsah was a town on the Euphrates River, far from Israel. Some ancient copies say “Tappuah,” and the Septuagint says “Tirzah.”
Pul was the Babylonian royal name of Tiglath-pileser III (verse 29).
The Hebrew says “a thousand talents of silver.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so this was about 34,000 kilograms.
The Hebrew says “fifty shekels of silver.” A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so this was about 575 grams.
Pekahiah means “Yahweh has opened (the eyes).”
Pekah means “he has opened (the eyes).”
The Hebrew words “with Argob and Arieh” are hard to understand. They may be names of men killed with the king, or names of places, and may belong with verse 29.
Tiglath-pileser III ruled Assyria from about 745 to 727 B.C.
Hoshea means “salvation.”
Rezin is probably Aramaic for “pleasing” or “prince.”
Ahaz means “he has grasped.” It is a short form of Jehoahaz.

verses.text: Ahaz son of Jotham began his rule over Judah when Pekah son of Remaliah had ruled Israel for seventeen years.
Ahaz took the throne at twenty and ruled sixteen years from Jerusalem. His ancestor David had pleased Yahweh his God, but Ahaz did not.

Instead he followed the ways of Israel’s kings. He even gave his own son to be burned as a sacrifice.{a} He copied the disgusting practices of the nations that Yahweh had pushed out ahead of the Israelites.
At the hilltop shrines, on the hilltops, and in the shade of every leafy tree, he offered sacrifices and burned incense.
Then Rezin, Aram’s king, and Pekah son of Remaliah, Israel’s king, came to fight against Jerusalem. They closed in around Ahaz there, but they could not beat him.{b}
At that time Rezin, Aram’s king,{c} won Elath back for Aram. He forced the people of Judah out of Elath. Edomites{d} came and settled in Elath, and it has been their home ever since.
Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, the Assyrian king. “I am your servant,” he said. “I am like your son. Aram’s king and Israel’s king have come against me. Come and save me from their power.”
Ahaz took the silver and gold from Yahweh’s temple and from the palace storerooms. He sent it to Assyria’s king as a gift.{e}
The Assyrian king agreed to help. He attacked Damascus and took it. He sent its people away as captives to Kir,{f} and he killed Rezin.
Then Ahaz went to Damascus for a meeting with Tiglath-pileser, Assyria’s king. While there, he saw an altar. He sent Uriah{g} the priest a drawing of it, with a careful plan of how it was made.
So Uriah the priest followed every detail the king had sent him from Damascus, and he built the altar to match. Uriah had it ready before the king got home.
Back from his trip, the king looked over the new altar. He went up to it and climbed its steps.
He offered his burnt offering and his grain offering on it. He poured out his drink offering. He splashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
Then he moved the old bronze altar, which stood before Yahweh. It had been between the new altar and Yahweh’s temple. Ahaz had it moved to the north side of his new altar.

Then the king commanded Uriah: “Use the big new altar for the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering. Offer the king’s burnt offering and grain offering on it. Offer there the burnt offerings, grain offerings and drink offerings of all the people of the land. Throw the blood of every animal offered against this altar. But I will use the bronze altar to ask for guidance.”{h}
Uriah the priest did all King Ahaz told him to do.

King Ahaz cut off the side panels from the movable stands and removed the washbasins from them. He lifted the huge bronze bowl called the Sea down from the twelve bronze bulls under it. He set it on a base of stone.
To please the king of Assyria, he also took away from Yahweh’s temple the covered walkway used on the Sabbath.{i} He removed the king’s outside entrance too.
The other things Ahaz did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Ahaz rested with his ancestors. He was laid in a grave among them in David’s City. His son Hezekiah{j} became king after him.

notes.text: That is, he offered his son as a burnt sacrifice. Compare 3:27 and Deuteronomy 18:10.
Compare Isaiah 7:1-9.
Many experts think “Rezin, Aram’s king” was added later, and that “Aram” here should be “Edom,” because the two words look alike in Hebrew.
The Hebrew read aloud and the Septuagint say “Edomites.” The written Hebrew says “Arameans.”
Or “a bribe.”
Kir was the land the Arameans first came from (Amos 9:7). No one knows where it was.
Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
Or “for me to think about.” The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
This follows the Hebrew read aloud. The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint says “a base for the throne.”
Hezekiah means “Yahweh makes strong.”

verses.text: Hoshea son of Elah became Israel’s king in Samaria when Ahaz had ruled Judah for twelve years. Hoshea ruled for nine years.
Yahweh saw that he did evil, though the kings of Israel before him had been worse.
Shalmaneser,{a} king of Assyria, marched against Hoshea. Hoshea gave in. He became Shalmaneser’s servant and paid him a tax every year.

But later the Assyrian king found out that Hoshea was plotting against him. Hoshea had sent messengers to So,{b} Egypt’s king, asking for help, and he had stopped paying the yearly tax to Assyria. So Assyria’s king arrested Hoshea and put him in prison.
Then the Assyrian king marched through the whole country. Samaria was surrounded by his army, and for three years he kept it shut in.

In the ninth year of Hoshea’s rule, Samaria fell to Assyria’s king. He carried the people of Israel off to his own land. He settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in towns where the Medes{c} lived.

All this happened because Israel’s people did wrong against Yahweh their God. He had brought them out of Egypt, setting them free from the power of Pharaoh, Egypt’s king. Yet they worshiped other gods.
They followed the ways of the nations Yahweh had chased out ahead of them. They also followed the practices that Israel’s kings had started.{d}

The Israelites secretly{e} did things that Yahweh their God said were wrong. They built hilltop shrines for themselves in all their towns, everywhere from the smallest lookout tower to the biggest walled city.
On every tall hill and under every green tree, they set up stone pillars and Asherah poles.
They burned incense at all the hilltop shrines, as the nations had done that Yahweh had driven away before them. They did evil things that made Yahweh angry.
They worshiped idols,{f} even though Yahweh had told them, “Do not do this.”

Through all his prophets and seers, Yahweh had given warnings to both Israel and Judah. “Turn away from your evil ways,” he said. “Keep my commands and my laws. Follow the whole Law that I gave to your ancestors, the Law I sent to you through my servants the prophets.”
They refused to hear. Like their ancestors, they were stiff-necked and stubborn. Those ancestors had not trusted Yahweh their God either.

They threw away his laws and the solemn promise he had made with their fathers. They ignored his warnings. They chased after worthless idols and became worthless themselves.{g} They copied the nations around them, though Yahweh had told them not to act like those nations.

They turned away from all the commands of Yahweh their God. They melted metal and made two calf idols. They made an Asherah pole. The sun, moon and stars received their worship. Baal became their master.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire. They tried to learn the future by magic and signs. They gave themselves over to doing what Yahweh saw as evil, and they made him angry.
Yahweh’s anger burned hot against Israel, and he sent them away from his presence. Only the tribe of Judah was left.
Yet Judah too broke the commands of Yahweh, their God. They took up the customs Israel had begun.
So Yahweh turned away from all of Israel’s people. He made them suffer and let robbers attack them. In the end he threw them out of his sight.
Yahweh had torn Israel away from David’s family. The people then crowned Nebat’s son Jeroboam as their king. Jeroboam pulled Israel away from following Yahweh and led them into a terrible sin.
The Israelites kept doing all the sins Jeroboam did. They did not stop.

At last Yahweh removed Israel from his presence. He had warned them through all his servants the prophets that he would do this. So Israel was taken out of their own land as captives to Assyria, and they are still there today.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim.{h} He moved them into Samaria’s towns to replace the Israelites. Samaria became theirs, and they made its towns their home.
At first these newcomers did not honor Yahweh. So Yahweh sent lions in among them, and some of them were killed.

A message was sent to Assyria’s king: “You moved people into the towns of Samaria. But these people do not know what the god of that land requires.{i} So he has let lions loose on them, and people are dying. They do not know how that god wants to be worshiped.”
Then the Assyrian king gave an order. “One of the priests we carried off from there must go back. Let him live there again and show the people the way the god of that land must be worshiped.”
So a priest who had been taken from Samaria returned. He made his home in Bethel and showed the people how to honor Yahweh.
But each group of people still made its own gods. They placed them in the shrines the Samarians had built on the hilltops. Every nation did this in its own towns.
Those who came from Babylon made Succoth-benoth. Nergal was made by those from Cuth, and Ashima by those from Hamath.
Nibhaz and Tartak were the gods of the Avvites. The Sepharvites even threw their sons and daughters into the fire for Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods they had brought with them.{j}
They worshiped Yahweh too. But they chose all kinds of people from among themselves to be priests at the hilltop shrines. These priests offered sacrifices for them in the shrines.
So they worshiped Yahweh, and at the same time they served their own gods. They kept the customs of the countries they had been taken away from.

Even now they keep doing things the old way. They do not truly worship Yahweh. They do not obey the laws, rules, teachings and commands that Yahweh gave to the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.{k}
Yahweh had made an agreement with them, and he had given them this command: “Other gods are not for you. You must never bow to them, serve them, or bring them sacrifices.
Worship only Yahweh, who brought you up out of Egypt by his mighty power and his strong arm. Bow down to him, and offer sacrifices to him.
Always be careful to obey the laws, rules, teachings and commands he wrote down for you. Do not worship other gods.
Remember the agreement I made with you. Never worship other gods.
Honor Yahweh your God alone. Then he will set you free from every enemy you have.”
But they would not listen. They kept doing things the old way.
So these nations worshiped Yahweh, but they also served their idols. Even today their children and grandchildren do what their ancestors did.

notes.text: Shalmaneser V ruled Assyria from about 727 to 722 B.C.
So may be the name of a pharaoh, perhaps Osorkon IV. Or it may be a place name, Sais, in the Nile delta.
The Septuagint says “the mountains of the Medes.”
The Hebrew here is awkward. It may mean “and the practices of the kings of Israel, which they followed.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain. It may mean “said false things about.”
The Hebrew word is gillulim, an insulting word for idols, perhaps meaning “dung balls.”
The Hebrew word is hebel, “vapor” or “breath.” It is a play on the idea of being worthless.
These were cities in Mesopotamia and Syria.
The Hebrew word is mishpat, here meaning “custom” or “required worship.” The same word is in verses 27, 33, 34 and 40.
Most of the gods named in verses 30-31 are not well known. Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of the underworld.
Verse 34 seems to disagree with verses 32-33. It may mean that these people did not worship Yahweh the way the Law required. Jacob was given the name Israel in Genesis 32:28.

verses.text: Hezekiah son of Ahaz started to rule Judah in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, who ruled Israel.
At twenty-five Hezekiah was crowned, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. Abi,{a} Zechariah’s daughter, was his mother.
Hezekiah did what pleased Yahweh. In every way he lived as his ancestor David had.

He got rid of the hilltop shrines. He broke the stone pillars to pieces and chopped down the Asherah pole. There was also a bronze snake that Moses had made long ago. Hezekiah smashed it, because the people of Israel had kept on offering incense to it up to that time. They called it Nehushtan.{b}
Hezekiah put his trust in Yahweh, Israel’s God. No king of Judah who came before him or after him was his equal.
He clung to Yahweh and never stopped following him. Every command that Yahweh gave Moses, Hezekiah kept.
Yahweh was with Hezekiah, and everything he set out to do went well. He refused to serve Assyria’s king and broke free from him.
He beat the Philistines and pushed them back as far as Gaza and the land around it. He took everything from their lookout towers to their walled cities.
In King Hezekiah’s fourth year, Shalmaneser, Assyria’s king, attacked Samaria and surrounded it. In Israel it was Hoshea’s seventh year as king.
Three years later the Assyrians took the city. Samaria fell in Hezekiah’s sixth year, Hoshea’s ninth.
Assyria’s king carried the Israelites off to his country. He sent them to live in Halah, in Gozan beside the Habor River, and among the Medes in their cities.
All of this came on them for refusing to obey Yahweh their God. They broke his agreement and everything Moses, Yahweh’s servant, had commanded. They closed their ears and would not do what he said.
In Hezekiah’s fourteenth year as king, Sennacherib,{c} king of Assyria, marched against all the walled cities of Judah and captured them.

So Hezekiah sent word to Lachish, where Assyria’s king was camped. “I was wrong,” he said. “Please leave my land. Whatever price you set, I will pay.” Assyria’s king demanded about 11 tons of silver from Hezekiah and about 1 ton of gold.{d}
Hezekiah handed over every bit of silver in Yahweh’s temple and in the palace storerooms.
Hezekiah had once covered the doors and doorposts of Yahweh’s temple with gold. Now he stripped off that gold and gave it to Assyria’s king.

But from Lachish the Assyrian king sent three of his highest officers, the Tartan, the Rab-saris and the Rabshakeh,{e} to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. A large army came with them. They marched up to Jerusalem and stopped beside the water channel from the Upper Pool, along the road to the field where cloth is washed.
They called for the king. Three men came out to them. One was Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who managed the palace. Shebnah, the royal writer, and Joah son of Asaph, who kept the records, came with him.
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Give Hezekiah this message from the great king, Assyria’s king: ‘What makes you feel so safe?
You claim to have good plans and a strong army. But your words mean nothing. Who are you counting on, now that you have turned against me?
Egypt? Egypt is like a broken reed. Lean on it like a walking stick, and it will cut your hand open. That is what Pharaoh, Egypt’s king, does to anyone who depends on him.
Or maybe you will tell me, “We trust Yahweh our God.” But Hezekiah tore down his hilltop shrines and altars! He ordered Judah and Jerusalem to worship at one altar only, the one in Jerusalem.
So come, make a bet with my master, Assyria’s king. I will hand over 2,000 horses to you. But I doubt you have 2,000 men who know how to ride!
You cannot drive back even one of my master’s lowest officers. So why depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
And do not suppose that Yahweh is against my coming here to wipe this place out. Yahweh himself said to me, “Attack this land and destroy it.”’”

Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebnah and Joah spoke up. “Please speak to us, your servants, in Aramaic,” they said to the Rabshakeh. “We can understand it. Do not use our own language{f} where the people on the wall can hear you.”

But the Rabshakeh answered, “My master did not send me to say these things only to your master and to you. I am talking to those men sitting on the wall. They are trapped with you. Before long, hunger will drive them, and you too, to feed on their own filth and to swallow their own urine.”{g}
Then the Rabshakeh stood up and shouted at the top of his voice in the Judeans’ language: “Hear the words of Assyria’s king, the great king!
He says, ‘Do not be fooled by Hezekiah. He cannot rescue you from my power.
Do not let Hezekiah talk you into trusting Yahweh. He says, “Yahweh will surely save us. Assyria’s king will never get this city.”

Do not listen to Hezekiah. Assyria’s king says this: “Make peace with me{h} and come out to me. Then each of you can eat grapes from his own vine and figs from his own tree. Each of you can drink water from his own well.

Later I will move you to a country like your own. There you will find fields of grain, new wine, bread, vineyards, olive trees and honey. Choose life, not death! Do not listen to Hezekiah when he fools you, saying, ‘Yahweh will save us.’
Name one nation whose god kept its land safe from Assyria’s king.
What became of the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah? Did they save Samaria from me?
Not one god of any land has saved his people from me. How then could Yahweh save Jerusalem from me?”’”
But the people kept quiet. They did not say a single word in reply, because the king had ordered, “Do not answer him.”

The three officials tore their clothes and went to Hezekiah: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace manager; Shebna, the royal writer; and Joah son of Asaph, the record keeper. They reported every word the Rabshakeh had spoken.

notes.text: Abi is a short form of Abijah, “Yahweh is my father” (2 Chronicles 29:1).
Nehushtan sounds like the Hebrew words nehosheth, “bronze,” and nahash, “snake.” Compare Numbers 21:8-9.
Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 B.C. He attacked Judah in 701 B.C.
The Hebrew says “three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so this was about 10,200 kilograms of silver and 1,020 kilograms of gold.
These are Assyrian titles. Tartan means “top commander.” Rab-saris means “chief officer.” Rabshakeh means “chief cupbearer” or field commander.
The Hebrew says “in Judean.” The same is true in verse 28.
The Hebrew read aloud has these words. The written Hebrew uses cruder words.
The Hebrew says “Make a blessing with me.”

subheads.26: The Field Commander Shouts to the People

verses.text: King Hezekiah heard their report. He tore his clothes, put on rough sackcloth, and went into Yahweh’s temple.
He sent Eliakim, the palace manager, and Shebna, the royal writer, with the older priests to see the prophet Isaiah{a} son of Amoz. All of them were wearing sackcloth.
They gave Isaiah this message: “Hezekiah says, ‘Today is a day of pain and shame. God is correcting us. We are like a woman ready to give birth, who has no strength left to push the baby out.

Assyria’s king sent his field commander to insult the living God. Maybe Yahweh your God has heard every word he said. Maybe Yahweh will punish him for those words. So please pray for the people who are still left here.’”
So King Hezekiah’s officials came to Isaiah,
and Isaiah told them, “Give your master this answer: ‘Yahweh says, “Do not let the words you heard frighten you. The servants of Assyria’s king have spoken against me, but do not be afraid.
Listen! I will put a spirit in him. He will hear news that makes him go home. Then I will make him die by the sword in his own country.”’”
The field commander left Jerusalem. He heard that Assyria’s king had moved on from Lachish. He caught up with the king at Libnah, where he was fighting.
Then news came to Sennacherib about Tirhakah,{b} the king of Cush.{c} “Tirhakah is marching out to fight you,” he was told. So Sennacherib sent messengers once more to Hezekiah.
“Speak to Hezekiah, Judah’s king,” he said. “Tell him, ‘You trust in your God, but he is tricking you. He promises that Assyria’s king will never capture Jerusalem. Do not believe it.
You know what the kings of Assyria have done to other countries. They wiped them out completely. Why would you be the only one to escape?
My fathers destroyed many peoples: Gozan, Haran and Rezeph, and Eden’s people in Telassar. Their gods did not save them, did they?
What has become of the kings of Hamath and Arpad? And the kings of Sepharvaim, of Hena, of Ivvah, where are they?’”
The messengers handed Hezekiah the letter, and he read it through. Then he went up to Yahweh’s temple. He opened the letter and laid it out in front of Yahweh.

Then Hezekiah prayed to Yahweh. “Yahweh, Israel’s God,” he said, “you sit on your throne between the winged creatures. You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. Heaven and earth are the work of your hands.
Yahweh, turn your ear toward me and listen. Yahweh, open your eyes and look. Hear the message Sennacherib has sent to make fun of the living God.
Yahweh, it is true that Assyria’s kings have destroyed these nations and their lands.
They have tossed the gods of those nations into flames. But those were not gods. People made them out of wood and stone with their own hands. So the Assyrians were able to wipe them out.
Yahweh our God, I beg you now to rescue us from his hand. Let all the kingdoms of the world learn that you alone, Yahweh, are God.”
A message then came to Hezekiah from Isaiah, Amoz’s son. “Yahweh, Israel’s God, says this: ‘You prayed to me about Sennacherib, Assyria’s king. I have heard you.’

Here is what Yahweh has said against Sennacherib:
‘The young woman Zion looks down on you.
She laughs at you.
The daughter Jerusalem shakes her head
at you as you run away.

Who have you insulted? Who have you mocked?
Against whom did you raise your voice?
You looked with proud eyes
at the Holy One of Israel!

I dug wells in foreign lands
and drank their water.
I marched through Egypt’s streams,
and under my feet they all went dry.”{g}

Haven’t you heard?
I planned it long ago.
In days long past I decided it.
Now I have made it happen.
That is why you have turned strong cities
into piles of stones.

Their people had no power left.
They were frightened and ashamed.
They were like plants in a field,
like new green shoots,
like grass growing on a roof,
dried up before it can grow tall.{h}

I know when you sit down.
I know when you go out and when you come in.
I know all about your fury against me.

Your fury and your pride
have reached my ears.
So I will put my hook in your nose
and my bit in your mouth.
I will turn you around
and send you back on the road you came by.’

“Hezekiah, here is the sign for you. For the rest of this year, your food will be grain that sprouts on its own. The year after, you will live on what comes up from that. The third year, sow your seed and gather your harvest once more. Plant vineyards and eat their grapes.
Those who are left alive in Judah will grow again like a plant. Their roots will go deep, and fruit will grow on their branches.
A group of people who survive will come out of Jerusalem. Those who escape will come from Mount Zion. Yahweh’s{i} burning love for his people will make this happen.

“Here then is Yahweh’s word about the king of Assyria:
‘This city will never see him inside it.
Not one of his arrows will fly into it.
No soldier with a shield will come near it.
No ramp of dirt will be piled up against it.

He will return by the road he took to get here.
He will not come into this city,
says Yahweh.

I will guard this city and save it,
for my own honor
and for my servant David.’”
That same night, out went the angel of Yahweh to the camp of the Assyrians. He struck down 185,000 of their men. When the others{j} woke up early the next morning, dead bodies lay everywhere.
So Sennacherib, Assyria’s king, packed up his camp and left. He went home and stayed in Nineveh.

Sennacherib went to worship Nisroch,{k} his god, in his temple. While he was bowed down there, Adrammelech and Sharezer, two of his own sons, struck him dead with swords. The murderers fled to Ararat.{l} Esarhaddon,{m} another son, took the throne.

notes.text: Isaiah means “Yahweh saves.”
Tirhakah (Taharqa) was a ruler from Cush who later became Egypt’s king. Here he was probably still commander of the army.
That is, the upper Nile region (modern Sudan).
The Hebrew word here is Adonai.
The Hebrew read aloud and the Septuagint say this. The written Hebrew says “With the chariot of my chariots.”
The Hebrew says “the forest of its Carmel,” meaning its garden land.
The Hebrew word here is Matsor, a name for Egypt used in poetry. It can also mean “attack on a city.”
The Hebrew says this, but the meaning is uncertain. Isaiah 37:27 and some ancient copies say “like a field with terraces.”
The Septuagint says “Yahweh of Armies,” as in Isaiah 37:32.
The Hebrew says “they.”
Nisroch is not known from any other place. The name may be a copying mistake for Nusku or Marduk.
Ararat is Urartu, in the area of modern Armenia.
Esarhaddon ruled Assyria from 681 to 669 B.C.

verses.text: About that time Hezekiah became very sick, so sick he was about to die. Isaiah, the prophet, Amoz’s son, came to see him. “Yahweh says, ‘Put your affairs in order,’” Isaiah told him. “‘Your life is ending. You will not get over this sickness.’”
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall. Then he prayed this prayer to Yahweh:
“Please, Yahweh,” he said, “remember how faithfully I have lived before you. My whole heart has been yours. My life has been spent doing what pleases you.” Then Hezekiah cried and cried.
Isaiah was leaving. But before he had passed the middle courtyard,{a} Yahweh spoke to him.

“Turn around,” he said. “Return to the palace and speak to my people’s ruler, Hezekiah. Say, ‘Yahweh, the God your ancestor David served, has a message for you. Your prayer has reached me, and I have seen you weep. I will make you well. On the third day from now you will go up to Yahweh’s temple.

I will give you fifteen more years to live. Assyria’s king will not take you or this city, for I will set you both free. I will be this city’s shield, both because of my own name and because of David, who served me.’”
Then Isaiah said, “Make a paste out of figs.” They did, and spread it on the sore. Then Hezekiah got better.
Earlier Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “How can I be sure Yahweh will heal me? What sign will show me that I will be in his temple two days from now?”
Isaiah had answered, “Yahweh will give you a sign to prove he will keep his promise. Do you want the shadow on the stairs to go ahead ten steps,{b} or back ten steps?”
“A shadow moving forward ten steps is nothing unusual,” Hezekiah said. “Make it go backward ten steps instead.”
Then Isaiah the prophet cried out to Yahweh. And Yahweh pulled the shadow back ten steps, up the stairway of Ahaz, the way it had already come down.
Around that time, Berodach-baladan{c} son of Baladan, Babylon’s king, heard that Hezekiah had been sick. He sent him letters and a gift.

Hezekiah gladly received{d} the messengers. He gave them a tour of his storehouses. He showed them his silver and gold, his spices and his fine olive oil. He showed them where his weapons were kept and all his other treasures. In his whole palace and kingdom there was nothing Hezekiah did not let them see.
Then Isaiah went to see the king. “Where did those men come from?” he asked. “What did they tell you?” Hezekiah said, “They came to me from a faraway country, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What did they look at in your palace?” “All of it,” Hezekiah said. “There is not one treasure of mine they did not see.”
Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Now hear what Yahweh says.

Someday soon, the whole wealth of your palace will be hauled away to Babylon. That includes all the treasures your ancestors have stored up to this day. Not a thing will be left. That is what Yahweh says.

Some of the sons who will come from your own family line will be taken away too. They will become palace servants, and their bodies will be cut so they can have no children. Babylon’s king will make them work for him in his palace.”
“What Yahweh has told me through you is good,” Hezekiah said to Isaiah. He was thinking, “At least there will be peace and safety while I am alive.”
The other events of Hezekiah’s rule, all his great deeds, are written in the official history of Judah’s kings. It describes the pool he built, and the tunnel{e} he dug to carry water into Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah died and was laid to rest. Manasseh,{f} his son, ruled in his place.

notes.text: The Hebrew read aloud and the Septuagint say “courtyard.” The written Hebrew says “the middle city.”
Or “degrees.” The Hebrew word maaloth means steps on a stairway that were used to tell time by the shadow.
Isaiah 39:1 and the Septuagint say “Merodach-baladan.” The name is Babylonian Marduk-apla-iddina, “Marduk has given an heir.”
The Hebrew says “listened to.” The Septuagint and Isaiah 39:2 say “was glad about.”
This was the tunnel cut through rock to bring water from the Gihon spring into the city. Today it is called Hezekiah’s Tunnel.
Manasseh means “making to forget.”

verses.text: Manasseh was a boy of twelve when he was crowned. His reign in Jerusalem lasted fifty-five years. Hephzibah{a} was his mother.
Manasseh did what Yahweh saw as evil. He copied the disgusting ways of the nations that Yahweh had pushed out of the land ahead of Israel.

His father Hezekiah had wrecked the hilltop shrines, but Manasseh built them again. He set up altars for Baal and made an Asherah pole,{b} the same as Ahab, Israel’s king, had done. He bowed in worship to the sun, moon and stars and served them.
He even built altars inside Yahweh’s temple. Yet this was the place Yahweh had chosen when he said, “Jerusalem is where I will put my name.”
In the two courtyards of Yahweh’s temple he built altars to worship the stars of the sky.

Even his own son he offered up in the fire.{c} He used magic and looked for signs to learn the future. He went to people who talked with the spirits of the dead. Again and again he did what Yahweh hated, stirring up his anger.

Manasseh carved an image of Asherah. He put it in Yahweh’s temple. Yet Yahweh had told David and his son Solomon about this temple. He had said, “This house, and Jerusalem, is where my name will stay forever. I picked this city out of all Israel’s tribes.
If the Israelites will be careful to do all I have commanded them, I will not make them leave this land again. I gave it to their ancestors. They must keep the whole Law my servant Moses gave them.”
But the people refused to listen. Manasseh led them astray. They did more evil than the nations Yahweh had destroyed as the Israelites came in.
So Yahweh gave this message through his servants the prophets:
“Manasseh, Judah’s king, has done these disgusting things. He has done worse than the Amorites who lived here before him. His idols{d} have pulled Judah into sin along with him.
So Yahweh, Israel’s God, says this: ‘Listen! I am sending a disaster on Jerusalem and Judah so terrible that anyone who hears the news will be shocked, as if both ears were ringing.

I will judge Jerusalem by the same measuring line I used on Samaria. I will test it with the plumb line I used on Ahab’s family.{e} I will wipe Jerusalem out the way someone wipes a bowl clean and then turns it upside down.
I will give up the people who are left of my own nation. Their enemies will take them, and every foe will loot and plunder them.
They have done what I see as evil. Ever since their ancestors left Egypt, right up to this day, they have kept on making me angry.’”
Manasseh also killed so many innocent people that their blood filled Jerusalem from one end to the other. On top of that, he caused Judah to sin and do what Yahweh saw as evil.
The other events of Manasseh’s rule, everything he did, including his sin, are written down in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Manasseh was laid to rest with his ancestors. They buried him in Uzza’s garden, which belonged to his palace. His son Amon{f} took the throne after him.
Amon was crowned at twenty-two. He ruled from Jerusalem for only two years. Meshullemeth,{g} Haruz’s daughter, was his mother. She came from Jotbah.
Amon did what Yahweh saw as evil, the same as his father Manasseh.
He lived just like his father in every way. The idols his father served, Amon served too, and he bowed low before them.
He walked away from Yahweh, the God of his ancestors. He would not live the way Yahweh wanted.
Some of Amon’s officials made a plot against him. Inside his own house they took his life.
The people of the land then executed everyone who had taken part in the plot against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah{h} king in his place.
The other things Amon did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Amon was laid in his tomb in the garden of Uzza. Josiah, his son, then ruled.

notes.text: Hephzibah means “my delight is in her.”
This was a wooden object used in the worship of the goddess Asherah.
Some ancient copies, including the Septuagint, say “his sons.” The Hebrew says “made his son pass through the fire,” which probably means child sacrifice.
The Hebrew word gillulim is an insulting word for idols, perhaps meaning “dung balls.”
The measuring line and plumb line are builders’ tools. They are a picture of judging Jerusalem by the same standard used for Samaria and Ahab’s family.
Amon means “faithful” or “master builder.”
Meshullemeth means “one repaid” or “one at peace.”
Josiah means “Yahweh supports.”

verses.text: Josiah was eight years old when he was crowned, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jedidah,{a} whose father was Adaiah from Bozkath.
Josiah did what pleased Yahweh. He followed in his ancestor David’s footsteps. He never turned off that path, to one side or the other.
When Josiah had been king for eighteen years,{b} he sent Shaphan{c} to Yahweh’s temple. Shaphan was the royal secretary. His father was Azaliah, and his grandfather was Meshullam. The king told him,
“Go see Hilkiah{d} the high priest. Have him add up all the silver that people have given at Yahweh’s temple. The doorkeepers have been taking it in from the worshipers.
Then the silver must go to the men who oversee the repair work. They are to pay it out to the workers who are fixing Yahweh’s temple.
That means the woodworkers, the builders and the stone workers. Also have them buy wood and cut stones to repair the temple.
The men in charge do not have to report how they spend the silver. They are honest men.”
Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan the secretary, “In Yahweh’s temple I came across the Book of the Law!” He passed it to Shaphan, who read it through.
Next Shaphan went to the king with news. “Your servants have taken the silver out of the temple,” he said. “They have turned it over to the men who are in charge of the work on Yahweh’s temple.”
Shaphan went on, “And Hilkiah the priest handed me a book.” Then Shaphan read it out loud in front of the king.
The king heard what the Book of the Law said. When he heard it, he tore his clothes.

Then the king called in Hilkiah the priest and Shaphan the secretary, along with Ahikam, Achbor{e} and Asaiah. (Ahikam’s father was Shaphan, Achbor’s father was Micaiah, and Asaiah was the king’s servant.) He told them,

“Go to Yahweh and ask him about the words in this book that was found. Ask on my behalf and on behalf of the people of Judah. Yahweh is very angry with us. Those who came before us paid no attention to what this book says. They failed to keep its commands, which were written for us.”

Off went Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan and Asaiah to see a woman named Huldah,{f} who was a prophet. Her husband was Shallum son of Tikvah and grandson of Harhas. Shallum looked after the royal robes. Her home was in Jerusalem’s newer section.{g} The men went and spoke with her there.
She said to them, “Yahweh, Israel’s God, says this: Go back to the man who sent you here. Tell him,
‘Yahweh says: Disaster is coming on this place and all who live in it. Everything written in the book that Judah’s king has read will happen.
They have left me behind. They have burned incense to other gods. All the idols they have made have stirred up my anger. So my anger will burn against this place like a fire that no one can put out.’
But the king of Judah sent you here to ask Yahweh what to do. Tell him, ‘Yahweh, Israel’s God, has this to say about the words you heard:

You heard me speak against this place and those living in it. I warned that they would be cursed and become a horror to others. Your heart was soft, and you made yourself humble before Yahweh. In sorrow you tore your robes, and your tears fell in my presence. So I have listened to you. That is what Yahweh says.
Because of that, you will join your ancestors in death and be buried in peace. You will not live to see the ruin I am going to bring here.’” So the men took her answer back to the king.

subheads.3: The Book of the Law Is Found

verses.text: The king called for all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to gather with him.

Then he went up to Yahweh’s temple. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem went too, with the priests and the prophets. Everyone came, from the least important to the most important. The king read the whole Book of the Agreement to them, the book that had been found in Yahweh’s temple.

The king stood beside the pillar. There, in front of Yahweh, he made a solemn promise. He would follow Yahweh. He would keep Yahweh’s commands, rules and laws with his whole heart and his whole being. He promised to do what this book said about the agreement. Every person there said yes to the agreement as well.

The king gave orders to Hilkiah the high priest, to the priests who served under him, and to the doorkeepers. “Remove from Yahweh’s temple everything made for Baal, for Asherah, and for the stars of the sky,” he said. They did, and he burned it all outside Jerusalem in the Kidron fields. The ashes he carried away to Bethel.

He got rid of the priests of false gods.{a} The kings of Judah had chosen these men to burn incense at the hilltop shrines in Judah’s towns and around Jerusalem. Josiah also got rid of the people who burned incense to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the star groups,{b} and to all the stars in the sky.
He took the Asherah pole out of Yahweh’s temple. He carried it outside Jerusalem to the Kidron Valley and burned it there. He ground it into dust and threw the dust on the graves of common people.
He tore down the rooms in Yahweh’s temple where the male shrine prostitutes{c} lived. Women had woven hangings{d} for Asherah in those rooms.

From all over Judah, Josiah had the priests come to Jerusalem. He made the hilltop shrines unfit for worship, the places where those priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba.{e} The gateway shrines{f} were torn down too. There was one at the entrance of the Gate of Joshua, the city governor. It stood on the left as you went through the city gate.
The priests of the hilltop shrines were not allowed to serve at Yahweh’s altar in Jerusalem. But they did eat bread made without yeast with the other priests.
Josiah made Topheth{g} unfit for worship. It lay in Ben-hinnom Valley. He did this so no one could ever again burn a son or daughter there as a sacrifice to Molech.

He took away the horses that Judah’s kings had given to honor the sun. They were kept at the entrance of Yahweh’s temple, in the open court{h} near the room of an official named Nathan-melech. He also burned the chariots used to worship the sun.

Judah’s kings had built altars on the roof near the upper room of Ahaz. Manasseh had built altars in the two courtyards of Yahweh’s temple. The king tore down all of them. He broke them up there{i} and dumped the rubble into the Kidron Valley.

Long ago Solomon, Israel’s king, had built hilltop shrines east of Jerusalem, on the south side of the Hill of Ruin.{j} He built them for Ashtoreth, the disgusting goddess of the people of Sidon. He built them for Chemosh, the disgusting god of Moab, and for Milcom, the hateful god of Ammon. Now the king made those shrines unfit for worship.
He broke the stone pillars to pieces and cut down the Asherah poles. He covered the places where they had stood with human bones.

Next Josiah tore down the altar at Bethel. Jeroboam son of Nebat had built that hilltop shrine, and he had led Israel into sin. Josiah tore down both the altar and the shrine. He set fire to the shrine and crushed it into powder. He burned the Asherah pole too.

Then Josiah turned and noticed tombs on the side of the hill. He sent men to take the bones out of the graves, and he burned them on the altar. That made the altar unfit for worship. This was what Yahweh had said would happen through a man of God long before.{k}

Josiah asked, “What is that stone I see there?” The people of the town said, “It marks the grave of the man of God from Judah. He spoke against the altar at Bethel and told about the very things you have done to it.”
“Let it stay as it is,” Josiah said. “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” So they did not touch his bones, or the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Israel’s kings had also put up hilltop shrines throughout the towns of Samaria. This had made Yahweh{l} angry. Josiah removed all those shrines too, as he had done at Bethel.
The priests who served at those shrines were put to death on the altars where they had served. Josiah burned dead men’s bones on those altars. Afterward he returned to Jerusalem.
Then the king ordered everyone, “Hold the Passover feast for Yahweh, your God. Do it the way this Book of the Agreement says.”
Such a Passover had not been held since the days when judges led Israel. None of the kings of Israel or Judah had held one like it.
But this Passover was held for Yahweh in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah.

Josiah also got rid of the people who talked with the dead and those who talked with spirits. He got rid of household gods,{m} idols and all the other disgusting things people worshiped in Judah and Jerusalem. In this way he carried out what the Law required. It was written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in Yahweh’s temple.
No king before Josiah had been like him, and none came after him. He turned to Yahweh with all his heart, all his soul and all his strength. He obeyed the whole Law of Moses.
Even so, Yahweh’s terrible anger against Judah did not cool. He was still angry because of everything Manasseh had done to stir him up.
Yahweh said, “I will remove Judah from my sight, as I removed Israel. I will turn away from Jerusalem, the city I chose. I will turn away from the temple. I said about it, ‘My name will be there.’”
The other things Josiah did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.

While Josiah was king, Pharaoh Neco,{n} Egypt’s king, led his army up to the Euphrates River to meet the king of Assyria.{o} Josiah led his own troops out to block the way. But when Neco saw him at Megiddo, he killed him.

Josiah’s servants carried his dead body by chariot from Megiddo back to Jerusalem. In his own tomb they laid him to rest. Then the people of the land chose Jehoahaz,{p} a son of Josiah. They anointed him with oil and crowned him as king in Josiah’s place.
Jehoahaz became king when he was twenty-three, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted three months. Hamutal was his mother. Her father was Jeremiah, and her hometown was Libnah.
Like his ancestors before him, Jehoahaz did evil in Yahweh’s eyes.
Pharaoh Neco locked him up at Riblah in the land of Hamath, so he could not rule in Jerusalem.{q} Neco made Judah pay about 3 3/4 tons of silver and about 75 pounds of gold.{r}
Then Pharaoh Neco crowned another son of Josiah, named Eliakim, in his father’s place. Neco gave Eliakim a new name, Jehoiakim.{s} As for Jehoahaz, Neco carried him off to Egypt, and he died there.
Jehoiakim gave Pharaoh all the silver and gold Pharaoh asked for. To get it, he taxed the land. He made each person pay silver and gold based on what they owned. Then he paid it to Pharaoh Neco.
Jehoiakim became king when he was twenty-five, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted eleven years. Zebidah was his mother. Her father was Pedaiah, and her hometown was Rumah.
Like his ancestors before him, Jehoiakim did evil in Yahweh’s eyes.

verses.text: While Jehoiakim was king, Nebuchadnezzar,{a} Babylon’s king, invaded the land. For three years Jehoiakim had to serve him. Then Jehoiakim turned against him and broke free.
So Yahweh sent bands of raiders against Jehoiakim. They came from Babylonia, Aram, Moab and Ammon. Yahweh sent them to wipe out Judah. He had said this would happen through his servants the prophets.
Yes, this happened to Judah because Yahweh commanded it. He was removing them from his sight because of all the sins Manasseh had done.
Manasseh had also killed innocent people, so many that Jerusalem was flooded with their blood. And Yahweh would not forgive that.
The other things Jehoiakim did are recorded in the official history of Judah’s kings.
Jehoiakim rested with his ancestors. His son Jehoiachin{b} took the throne.
After this, Egypt’s king did not lead his army out of his own land again. Babylon’s king had taken over everything that had been his, all the way from the Brook of Egypt{c} to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen when he was crowned, and he lasted only three months as king in Jerusalem. Nehushta{d} was his mother. Her father was Elnathan, and she came from Jerusalem.
Jehoiachin did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. He was just like his father in every way.
At that time the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon’s king, marched on Jerusalem and surrounded the city.
While his soldiers had the city closed in, Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived.

Then Jehoiachin, Judah’s king, went out and gave himself up to Babylon’s king. His mother, his servants, his commanders and his palace officials gave themselves up too. Babylon’s king made Jehoiachin his prisoner. This was in Nebuchadnezzar’s eighth year as king.{e}

Yahweh had warned that it would happen, and it did. Nebuchadnezzar carried away all the treasures from Yahweh’s temple and from the palace. He cut apart all the gold objects that Solomon, Israel’s king, had made for Yahweh’s temple.

He took away the people of Jerusalem as captives: every commander and every brave fighter, 10,000 people. He also took every skilled worker and metalworker.{f} Nobody stayed behind except the poorest of the poor.

Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin away to Babylon. He also took the king’s mother and his wives, his officials, and the most important men of the land. He led them all from Jerusalem into Babylon as captives.
The king of Babylon also forced 7,000 strong soldiers to go to Babylon. He took 1,000 skilled workers and metalworkers too. All of them were strong men, able to fight in a war.
Babylon’s king made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle,{g} king in Jehoiachin’s place. He changed Mattaniah’s name to Zedekiah.{h}
Zedekiah was crowned at twenty-one and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem. Hamutal{i} was his mother. Her father was Jeremiah, and she came from Libnah.
Zedekiah did evil in Yahweh’s eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done.
All this happened to Jerusalem and Judah because Yahweh was angry. In the end he threw them out of his presence. Then Zedekiah turned against Babylon’s king.

Jehoiachin means “Yahweh makes firm.” He is also called Jeconiah and Coniah.

verses.text: So Babylon’s king Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem, bringing all his troops. Zedekiah had been king for nine years. It was the tenth month (December-January),{a} on its tenth day. They set up camp around the city and built ramps all around it for the attack.
The army kept the city shut in until King Zedekiah had ruled eleven years.
By the fourth month (June-July),{b} on day nine, the hunger in the city was terrible. The common people had no food at all.

Then the enemy broke a hole in the city wall. All the soldiers ran away{c} at night, even though the Babylonians had surrounded the city. They slipped out by the gate that stood between the double walls, close to the royal garden. The king{d} fled toward the Jordan Valley.{e}
But the Babylonian army went after King Zedekiah. He was overtaken on the open plains of Jericho. All his soldiers had left him and scattered.
So they captured the king. They brought him to Babylon’s king at Riblah, and there he was judged and sentenced.
They made Zedekiah watch as his sons were put to death. Then they blinded Zedekiah, tied him up with bronze chains, and took him to Babylon.

Nebuzaradan{g} arrived in Jerusalem on day seven of the fifth month (July-August).{f} He was the commander of the royal guard and an officer of Babylon’s king. That was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar’s rule over Babylon.
Nebuzaradan set Yahweh’s temple on fire. He also burned the palace and the homes of Jerusalem. All the great buildings burned to the ground.
Then the Babylonian troops who came with the guard commander knocked down the walls that circled Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan, the guard commander, took away as captives the people still left in the city. He also took those who had gone over to Babylon’s side, along with all the rest of the people.{h}
But he let some of the poorest people stay. Their work would be to look after the grapevines and plow the fields.
The Babylonians broke the bronze pillars of Yahweh’s temple into pieces. They did the same to the movable stands and the huge bronze bowl called the Sea.{i} They carried the bronze to Babylon.
They took the bronze tools of temple worship as well: pots and shovels, dishes, and the trimmers for the lamp wicks.
The guard commander took the fire pans and the bowls for sprinkling. He took everything made of pure gold or pure silver.
Solomon had made the two pillars, the Sea and the movable stands for Yahweh’s temple. There was so much bronze in them that no one could weigh it.

Each pillar was 27 feet{j} tall. On top of each was a bronze cap 4 1/2 feet{k} tall. A net of bronze chains with bronze pomegranates went around the cap. The other pillar matched it exactly, net and all.
The guard commander also took prisoners. Among them were Seraiah, the chief priest, and Zephaniah, the priest next under him. He also took the three men who guarded the temple doors.

Out of the city he also took the officer who led the fighting men, and five of the king’s closest advisers{l} who were found there. Next came the secretary of the army commander,{m} who called up the people of the land for war. Sixty more common men found in the city were added to the group.
Nebuzaradan, the guard commander, led them all to Babylon’s king at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king ordered them struck down, and they died. That is how Judah was carried away from its own land.
Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon’s king, had left some people behind in Judah. He chose Gedaliah{n} to rule over them as governor. Gedaliah’s father was Ahikam, and his grandfather was Shaphan.

All the army officers and their men heard that Babylon’s king had made Gedaliah governor. They came with their troops to meet him at Mizpah. Ishmael, Nethaniah’s son, was there. So were Johanan, Kareah’s son, and Seraiah, Tanhumeth’s son, from Netophah. Jaazaniah, the son of the Maacathite, came too.

Gedaliah made a promise to the officers and their men. “You do not need to fear the Babylonian officials,” he said. “Stay here and live in this land. Serve Babylon’s king, and life will be good for you.”

The seventh month (September-October){o} brought a new disaster. Ishmael son of Nethaniah came with ten men. He was the grandson of Elishama and came from the royal family. They attacked Gedaliah and killed him. They also murdered everyone at Mizpah with him, both Judeans and Babylonians.
Then the whole population, from the least to the greatest, fled to Egypt along with the army officers. They feared the Babylonians and what they might do.

Jehoiachin, Judah’s king, had been a prisoner for thirty-seven years. In that year Evil-merodach{p} became Babylon’s king. On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month (February-March),{r} he set Jehoiachin free{q} from prison.
He spoke kindly to Jehoiachin. He set his seat higher than the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes. Each day, as long as he lived, he had his meals at the king’s table.
The king also provided Jehoiachin with a fixed amount of food and supplies, day after day. This went on as long as Jehoiachin lived.
